questions.question: When a solution of a primary standard is prepared for titration, which of the following is required?
questions.answer: A primary standard solution is made by accurately weighing the solid on an electronic balance, dissolving it and making it up to the mark in a volumetric flask. A burette, pipette and indicator are used in the titration itself, not in preparing the standard.

questions.question: What flame colour do copper ions produce when heated?
questions.answer: Copper ions give a blue-green flame. (Brick red = calcium, pale purple/lilac = potassium, yellow-orange = sodium.)

questions.question: Which list contains members of the same homologous series?
questions.answer: Members of a homologous series share a general formula and functional group and differ by $\text{CH}_2$ units. Ethane, butane and hexane all fit $\text{C}_n\text{H}_{2n+2}$ (alkanes). The other lists mix different general formulas or functional groups.

questions.question: Identify the correct balanced equation for the incomplete combustion of $\text{C}_4\text{H}_9\text{OH}$.
questions.answer: Incomplete combustion produces CO. Checking oxygen atoms in D: left $1 + 4\times 2 = 9$, right $4 + 5 = 9$ — balanced. B is unbalanced (left has $2 + 24 = 26$ O, right has $8 + 10 = 18$). A and C are complete combustion.

questions.question:
Belle studied the following equilibrium reaction:

$$\text{Fe}^{3+}(aq) + \text{SCN}^-(aq) \rightleftharpoons [\text{Fe(SCN)}]^{2+}(aq) \qquad \Delta H < 0$$

The concentration profile shown represents a change to this equilibrium system at time $t_1$: $[\text{SCN}^-]$ jumps up suddenly at $t_1$ and then decreases gradually, while $[\text{Fe}^{3+}]$ decreases gradually and $[\text{Fe(SCN)}]^{2+}$ increases gradually to new constant values.

Which one of the following would account for the changes in concentration at time $t_1$?
questions.answer: Only $[\text{SCN}^-]$ changes suddenly at $t_1$ (a sharp increase), so $\text{SCN}^-$ was added. By Le Chatelier's principle the system partly counteracts this by shifting right: $[\text{SCN}^-]$ and $[\text{Fe}^{3+}]$ then fall gradually and $[\text{Fe(SCN)}]^{2+}$ rises. A temperature change would not cause a sudden jump in any concentration.

questions.question:
For the equilibrium

$$\text{Fe}^{3+}(aq) + \text{SCN}^-(aq) \rightleftharpoons [\text{Fe(SCN)}]^{2+}(aq) \qquad \Delta H < 0$$

which one of the following best represents the changes in concentration when the equilibrium mixture is diluted at time $t_2$?
questions.answer: Dilution instantly lowers all three concentrations at $t_2$. The system then shifts to the side with more dissolved particles (2 on the left vs 1 on the right) to partly counteract the decrease, i.e. to the left. So after the sudden drop, $[\text{Fe(SCN)}]^{2+}$ decreases further while $[\text{Fe}^{3+}]$ and $[\text{SCN}^-]$ increase slightly — graph B. (Equivalently, the reaction quotient $Q = \frac{[\text{Fe(SCN)}^{2+}]}{[\text{Fe}^{3+}][\text{SCN}^-]}$ increases on dilution, so $Q > K_{eq}$ and the reverse reaction is favoured.)

questions.question: The graph shows the changes in pH during a titration. Which pH range should an indicator have to best determine the end point of this titration?
questions.answer: The curve starts at pH 14 and levels off at about pH 5, so a weak acid is being added to a strong base. The equivalence point (middle of the steep section) is basic, at roughly pH 9–10, so an indicator changing colour in the range 8.3–10.0 (e.g. phenolphthalein) is best.

questions.question: Which list consists of amphiprotic substances only?
questions.answer: An amphiprotic species can both donate and accept a proton. $\text{HCO}_3^-$ (→ $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$ or $\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3$), $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ (→ $\text{OH}^-$ or $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$) and $\text{HSO}_4^-$ (→ $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$ or $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$) all can. $\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3$ and $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ can only donate; $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$ can only accept.

questions.question:
Consider the following equilibrium:

$$\text{CH}_4(g) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(g) \rightleftharpoons 3\text{H}_2(g) + \text{CO}(g) \qquad \Delta H = +208\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$

Which statement best describes the effect of increasing temperature in terms of collision theory?
options: All reactant and product molecules have more energy and move more quickly; increased temperature has a greater effect on the exothermic reaction than the endothermic reaction and so the equilibrium shifts to the right.

All reactant and product molecules have more energy and move more quickly; increased temperature has a greater effect on the endothermic reaction than the exothermic reaction and so the equilibrium shifts to the right.

All reactant and product molecules have less energy and move more slowly; increased temperature has a greater effect on the endothermic reaction than the exothermic reaction and so the equilibrium shifts to the right.

All reactant and product molecules have less energy and move more quickly; increased temperature has a greater effect on the endothermic reaction than the exothermic reaction and so the equilibrium shifts to the left.
questions.answer: Heating gives all molecules more kinetic energy. The forward (endothermic) reaction has the higher activation energy, so the fraction of collisions exceeding it increases proportionally more than for the reverse (exothermic) reaction. The forward rate increases more, so the equilibrium shifts right.

questions.question:
Two titrations were performed. In each, 0.2 M NaOH solution in a burette was added to a conical flask: one flask contained 25.0 mL of 0.1 M strong monoprotic acid and the other 25.0 mL of 0.1 M weak monoprotic acid.

Which one of the following statements is true?
options: The weak acid will require a greater volume of NaOH solution than the strong acid to reach equivalence point.
The weak acid will require a smaller volume of NaOH solution than the strong acid to reach equivalence point.
The weak acid will require the same volume of NaOH solution as the strong acid to reach equivalence point.
The strong acid will require double the volume of NaOH solution as the weak acid to reach equivalence point.
questions.answer: Both flasks contain $n = 0.1 \times 0.0250 = 2.5 \times 10^{-3}$ mol of a monoprotic acid, which reacts 1 : 1 with NaOH. As the weak acid is neutralised its equilibrium shifts to release more $\text{H}^+$, so it is completely neutralised by the same amount of NaOH: both need $2.5 \times 10^{-3} / 0.2 = 12.5$ mL. Acid strength affects the pH, not the volume to equivalence.

questions.question:
A solution containing an unknown salt was tested using a number of steps. The table shows the tests carried out and the observed results.

| Step | Procedure | Results |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Added nitric acid | No reaction |
| 2 | Added barium nitrate | No reaction |
| 3 | Added silver nitrate | White precipitate formed |
| 4 | Added sodium sulfate to a fresh sample | No reaction |
| 5 | Added sodium hydroxide to a fresh sample | A green precipitate formed which turned brown on standing |

The student identified the salt as:
questions.answer: No reaction with nitric acid rules out carbonate; no precipitate with $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ rules out sulfate; a white precipitate with $\text{Ag}^+$ shows chloride (AgCl). With $\text{OH}^-$ a green precipitate of $\text{Fe(OH)}_2$ forms, which is oxidised in air to brown $\text{Fe(OH)}_3$ — so the cation is $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ (iron(III) would give a brown precipitate immediately). The salt is iron(II) chloride.

questions.question: Identify the correct conductometric titration curve (conductance against volume of NaOH added) for the titration of acetic acid with sodium hydroxide.
questions.answer: Acetic acid is weak, so the initial conductance is low and drops only slightly as the few $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ ions are neutralised; it then rises gradually as $\text{Na}^+$ and $\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-$ ions accumulate, and rises more steeply after the equivalence point because of excess highly mobile $\text{OH}^-$ ions. This shallow dip followed by an increasingly steep rise is graph D. (A is a strong acid/strong base curve; B and C level off, which cannot happen while excess $\text{OH}^-$ is being added.)

questions.question:
A 0.10 M solution of fluoride ions is gradually added to a solution containing $\text{Ba}^{2+}$, $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ and $\text{Pb}^{2+}$ ions, each at a concentration of 0.0010 M.

| Salt | $K_{sp}$ |
|---|---|
| $\text{BaF}_2$ | $1.8 \times 10^{-7}$ |
| $\text{CaF}_2$ | $1.5 \times 10^{-10}$ |
| $\text{PbF}_2$ | $7.1 \times 10^{-7}$ |

In what order, from first to last, will the precipitates of $\text{BaF}_2$, $\text{CaF}_2$ and $\text{PbF}_2$ form?
questions.answer:
A precipitate forms when $[\text{M}^{2+}][\text{F}^-]^2 > K_{sp}$, i.e. when $[\text{F}^-] > \sqrt{K_{sp}/0.0010}$:
- $\text{CaF}_2$: $\sqrt{1.5\times10^{-7}} = 3.9 \times 10^{-4}$ M
- $\text{BaF}_2$: $\sqrt{1.8\times10^{-4}} = 1.3 \times 10^{-2}$ M
- $\text{PbF}_2$: $\sqrt{7.1\times10^{-4}} = 2.7 \times 10^{-2}$ M

The salt needing the least fluoride precipitates first: $\text{CaF}_2$, then $\text{BaF}_2$, then $\text{PbF}_2$.

questions.question:
Mulan prepares a dilute solution of cobalt(II) chloride in a small beaker, stirring until it becomes a consistent colour. The equilibrium is endothermic as written below:

$$\underset{\text{pink}}{[\text{Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6]^{2+}(aq)} + 4\text{Cl}^-(aq) \rightleftharpoons \underset{\text{blue}}{[\text{CoCl}_4]^{2-}(aq)} + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$$

Mulan pours some of the solution into three separate test tubes. To the first test tube she adds some hydrochloric acid. To the second test tube she adds some silver nitrate solution, and a precipitate immediately forms. She places the third test tube in a larger beaker of ice water.

What would be the expected observations for test tube 1 (HCl added), test tube 2 ($\text{AgNO}_3$ added) and test tube 3 (ice bath)?
options: 1: more pink; 2: more blue; 3: more pink
1: more blue; 2: more pink; 3: more pink
1: more blue; 2: more blue; 3: more blue
1: more blue; 2: more pink; 3: more blue
questions.answer: 1: HCl adds $\text{Cl}^-$, so the equilibrium shifts right — more blue. 2: $\text{Ag}^+$ removes $\text{Cl}^-$ as AgCl precipitate, so the equilibrium shifts left — more pink. 3: the forward reaction is endothermic, so cooling shifts the equilibrium left (exothermic direction) — more pink.

questions.question:
A 2.45 g sample of a supermarket brand lawn fertiliser was analysed using gravimetric analysis for its sulfate content. After filtration and drying to constant mass, 2.18 g of barium sulfate was recovered.

What is the % w/w of sulfate in the fertiliser?

The graph shows the boiling points of four different organic compounds, I, II, III and IV: approximately $-100\ ^{\circ}\text{C}$, $20\ ^{\circ}\text{C}$, $78\ ^{\circ}\text{C}$ and $118\ ^{\circ}\text{C}$ respectively.

Which row correctly classifies the compounds based on their boiling points?
options: I ethane, II ethanal, III ethanol, IV ethanoic acid
I ethanal, II ethane, III ethanol, IV ethanoic acid
I ethanal, II ethane, III ethanoic acid, IV ethanol
I ethane, II ethanal, III ethanoic acid, IV ethanol
questions.answer: Ethane has only dispersion forces (lowest b.p.); ethanal adds dipole–dipole forces; ethanol forms hydrogen bonds; ethanoic acid forms the most extensive hydrogen bonding (two H-bonding sites, dimers), so it has the highest b.p. Order: ethane < ethanal < ethanol < ethanoic acid.

questions.question: Look at the structures I–IV shown. Which structure is that of 2,2,4-trimethylpentane?
questions.answer: 2,2,4-trimethylpentane is $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C–CH}_2\text{–CH(CH}_3)\text{–CH}_3$: a five-carbon chain with two methyls on one end carbon's neighbour (C2) and one on C4. II is exactly this, and III is the same molecule drawn from the other end. I and IV both have a six-carbon longest chain with methyls on C2 and C5 (2,5-dimethylhexane).

questions.question: The mass spectrum of pentan-3-one ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COCH}_2\text{CH}_3$) is shown. Which ion is responsible for the base peak in the mass spectrum of pentan-3-one?
questions.answer: The base peak (tallest) is at $m/z = 57$. $[\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CO}]^+$ has mass $29 + 28 = 57$ and forms by losing an ethyl group from the molecular ion ($m/z$ 86). ($[\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2]^+$ is the peak at 29; $[\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_2]^+$ cannot form from pentan-3-one, and $\text{C}_4\text{H}_9^+$ also has mass 57 but is not a fragment of this molecule.)

questions.question:
A green dye used to colour tinned peas is made by mixing the yellow chemical, curcumin, with another colouring agent called bright blue. The individual absorbance spectra of curcumin, bright blue and a typical green dye mixture are shown.

UV-Vis spectrometry was used to analyse the curcumin content of tinned peas. Identify the wavelength which would be best used for absorbance measurements to determine the curcumin content of the peas.
questions.answer: The wavelength must be strongly absorbed by curcumin but not by bright blue, so that the absorbance depends only on curcumin. At 400 nm curcumin absorbs strongly while bright blue's absorbance is almost zero. At 450 nm bright blue already absorbs noticeably, and at 575 and 700 nm bright blue dominates or nothing absorbs.

questions.question: What is the pH of the resulting solution when 50.0 mL of 0.600 mol L$^{-1}$ sodium hydroxide and 50.0 mL of 0.250 mol L$^{-1}$ sulfuric acid are mixed?
Jasmine and Ariel were curious if cherries could be used as a natural indicator. Outline how Jasmine and Ariel could both prepare and test a natural indicator made from cherries.
questions.answer:
**Preparation:** Cut up and crush a few cherries with a mortar and pestle in a small volume of distilled water (or gently heat them in water/ethanol) to extract the coloured pigment. Filter (or decant/pipette off) the coloured liquid to obtain a clear indicator solution.

**Testing:** Place about 1 mL of solutions of known pH covering the full range — e.g. pH 1, 3, 5, 7 (neutral), 9, 11 and 13 (buffers, or dilute HCl, distilled water and dilute NaOH) — into separate labelled test tubes. Add 2 drops of the cherry extract to each, mix and record the colour in each tube. If the colour changes clearly across the pH range, the extract works as an indicator, and the pH range over which the colour changes can be identified.

questions.question:
The Gunwinggu people in the Northern Territory eat the roots of a bitter yam plant, which they call mangindjeg. These roots contain salts (oxalates) that would be toxic if consumed raw.

Using this example OR another food prepared by Indigenous peoples, identify at least THREE steps in the preparation and explain how these steps effectively remove the toxins.
questions.answer:
1. **The yam roots are cut or ground up.** This increases the surface area in contact with water, so the soluble oxalate salts dissolve faster.
2. **The pieces are soaked in (running) water for a long time.** The oxalate toxins are soluble and leach out into the water. In still water a dissolution equilibrium is reached and no more toxin dissolves.
3. **The water is changed repeatedly (or the yam is placed in running water/rinsed).** Removing the toxin-laden water keeps the concentration of dissolved oxalate low, so by Le Chatelier's principle the equilibrium keeps shifting towards dissolution and more oxalate is leached out of the yam.
4. **The yam is then cooked (e.g. roasted or baked).** Heating breaks down or chemically changes remaining toxins, further detoxifying the food.

questions.question:
Initially a 2.00 L glass vessel contains a mixture of only 1.00 mole of hydrogen gas and 1.00 mole of iodine gas. The gases react as follows:

$$\text{H}_2(g) + \text{I}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{HI}(g)$$

At 400°C, equilibrium is achieved, and the concentration of hydrogen iodide gas is 0.760 mol L$^{-1}$.

Calculate the equilibrium constant for this reaction at 400°C and state what the value indicates about the reaction. Show all working.
questions.answer:
Initial concentrations: $[\text{H}_2] = [\text{I}_2] = \dfrac{1.00}{2.00} = 0.500$ mol L$^{-1}$.

| | $[\text{H}_2]$ | $[\text{I}_2]$ | $[\text{HI}]$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| Initial | 0.500 | 0.500 | 0 |
| Change | $-0.380$ | $-0.380$ | $+0.760$ |
| Equilibrium | 0.120 | 0.120 | 0.760 |

$$K_{eq} = \frac{[\text{HI}]^2}{[\text{H}_2][\text{I}_2]} = \frac{(0.760)^2}{(0.120)(0.120)} = 40.1$$

$K_{eq} > 1$ (moderately large), so at equilibrium at 400°C the products are favoured: the position of equilibrium lies to the right.

questions.question:
In an experiment to determine the enthalpy of combustion of propan-1-ol, $\text{C}_3\text{H}_7\text{OH}$, Anna heated water in a copper container (calorimeter), clamped to a retort stand, using a spirit burner containing propan-1-ol placed directly below it; a thermometer measured the water temperature.

Anna measured 50.0 mL of water into the copper calorimeter and lit the spirit burner. When the temperature of the water had gone up by 12.8°C, she found that 0.100 g of propan-1-ol had been burnt.

Calculate the molar enthalpy of combustion for propan-1-ol.
questions.answer:
Heat absorbed by the water ($m = 50.0$ g, $c = 4.18\ \text{J g}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$):

$$q = mc\Delta T = 50.0 \times 4.18 \times 12.8 = 2675\ \text{J} = 2.675\ \text{kJ}$$

$M(\text{C}_3\text{H}_7\text{OH}) = 3(12.01) + 8(1.008) + 16.00 = 60.09\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$, so

$$n = \frac{0.100}{60.09} = 1.664 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{mol}$$

$$\Delta_c H = -\frac{q}{n} = -\frac{2.675}{1.664 \times 10^{-3}} = -1.61 \times 10^{3}\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$

(negative because combustion is exothermic).

questions.question:
In an experiment to determine the enthalpy of combustion of propan-1-ol, $\text{C}_3\text{H}_7\text{OH}$, Anna heated water in a copper container (calorimeter), clamped to a retort stand, using a spirit burner containing propan-1-ol placed directly below it; a thermometer measured the water temperature.

Using $q = mc\Delta T$ and the mass of propan-1-ol burnt, Anna calculated the molar enthalpy of combustion. She used a draught shield the second time she carried out this experiment.

Identify how using a draught shield may affect the accuracy of her experimental data and state the effect on the calculated value of the enthalpy of combustion.
questions.answer: A draught shield reduces heat loss to the surroundings (it stops air currents carrying heat away and keeps the flame directed at the calorimeter), so more of the heat released by the burning propan-1-ol is absorbed by the water. The measured temperature rise is therefore larger for the same mass of fuel, making the data more accurate: the calculated molar enthalpy of combustion becomes larger in magnitude (more negative), closer to the theoretical value (about $-2021\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$).

questions.question:
Citronellol is a compound that is found in citronella oils. Its structural formula (skeletal) is shown: it is 3,7-dimethyloct-6-en-1-ol, $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C=CH–CH}_2\text{–CH}_2\text{–CH(CH}_3)\text{–CH}_2\text{–CH}_2\text{–OH}$.

Give the molecular formula of citronellol.
questions.answer: $\text{C}_{10}\text{H}_{20}\text{O}$ (also written $\text{C}_{10}\text{H}_{19}\text{OH}$).

questions.question:
Citronellol is a compound that is found in citronella oils. Its structural formula (skeletal) is shown: it is 3,7-dimethyloct-6-en-1-ol, $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C=CH–CH}_2\text{–CH}_2\text{–CH(CH}_3)\text{–CH}_2\text{–CH}_2\text{–OH}$.

Identify the two most prominent functional groups found in citronellol.
questions.answer: Hydroxyl group (alcohol, $-\text{OH}$) and carbon–carbon double bond (alkene, $\text{C=C}$).

questions.question:
Citronellol is a compound that is found in citronella oils. Its structural formula (skeletal) is shown: it is 3,7-dimethyloct-6-en-1-ol, $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C=CH–CH}_2\text{–CH}_2\text{–CH(CH}_3)\text{–CH}_2\text{–CH}_2\text{–OH}$.

Predict and justify the solubility of citronellol in water.
questions.answer:
**Prediction:** citronellol is only very slightly soluble in water.

**Justification:**
- The hydroxyl ($-\text{OH}$) group is polar because of the large electronegativity difference between O and H, so it can form hydrogen bonds with water molecules, which favours some solubility.
- However, the molecule has a large non-polar hydrocarbon chain (10 carbon atoms) that can only form dispersion forces. Water molecules cannot hydrogen bond with this part, and dissolving it would disrupt the hydrogen bonding between water molecules.
- Because the large hydrophobic part dominates the single $-\text{OH}$ group, citronellol is only very slightly soluble — far less soluble than small alcohols such as ethanol, which is miscible with water.

questions.question:
The concentration of copper ions in one sample of river water was determined by colorimetry. An almost colourless sample of the river water was complexed with excess ammonia to form a deep blue solution of copper tetraamine ions:

$$\text{Cu}^{2+}(aq) + 4\text{NH}_3(aq) \rightleftharpoons [\text{Cu(NH}_3)_4]^{2+}(aq)$$

A set of standards was produced, and the absorbance of each standard was measured:

| Concentration of $[\text{Cu(NH}_3)_4]^{2+}$ ions (ppm) | Absorbance |
|---|---|
| 0.0 | 0.000 |
| 5.0 | 0.120 |
| 10.0 | 0.219 |
| 15.0 | 0.325 |
| 20.0 | 0.450 |
| 25.0 | 0.567 |

Draw a calibration graph of the data.
questions.answer: Plot absorbance (vertical axis, 0 to 0.600) against concentration of $[\text{Cu(NH}_3)_4]^{2+}$ in ppm (horizontal axis, 0 to 30 ppm), with labelled axes including units and even scales. Plot the six points accurately and draw a single straight line of best fit through the origin (slope ≈ 0.0224 absorbance units per ppm) — do not join the dots.

questions.question:
The concentration of copper ions in one sample of river water was determined by colorimetry. An almost colourless sample of the river water was complexed with excess ammonia to form a deep blue solution of copper tetraamine ions:

$$\text{Cu}^{2+}(aq) + 4\text{NH}_3(aq) \rightleftharpoons [\text{Cu(NH}_3)_4]^{2+}(aq)$$

A set of standards was produced, and the absorbance of each standard was measured:

| Concentration of $[\text{Cu(NH}_3)_4]^{2+}$ ions (ppm) | Absorbance |
|---|---|
| 0.0 | 0.000 |
| 5.0 | 0.120 |
| 10.0 | 0.219 |
| 15.0 | 0.325 |
| 20.0 | 0.450 |
| 25.0 | 0.567 |

The intensity of the light after passing through the river-water sample was 42.6% of the incident intensity. The absorbance $A$ of the sample is given by

$$A = \log_{10}\frac{I_0}{I}$$

where $I_0$ is the intensity of the light before passing through the sample and $I$ is the intensity after passing through the sample.

Use the formula to determine the absorbance of the sample solution and hence, using a calibration graph of the data, calculate the concentration of copper ions in the original solution in mol L$^{-1}$.

The concentration of copper ions in a sample of river water was determined by colorimetry after complexing the $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ ions with excess ammonia to form deep blue $[\text{Cu(NH}_3)_4]^{2+}$. Outline an alternative technique to colorimetry that could be used to accurately determine the concentration of copper ions if ammonia was not available.
questions.answer: **Atomic absorption spectroscopy (AAS).** The sample solution is sprayed into a hot flame, where it is vaporised and atomised. Light from a copper hollow-cathode lamp, of a wavelength specific to copper atoms, passes through the flame and is absorbed by the copper atoms' electrons; a monochromator selects that wavelength and a detector measures how much light is absorbed. The absorbance is proportional to the copper concentration, which is found by comparing it with a calibration curve made from copper standards. AAS is very sensitive (ppm–ppb) and specific to copper, so no complexing agent is needed.

questions.question:
The flow chart shows reactions of a range of organic compounds, all linked to propan-1-ol, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$:
- Compound A $\xrightarrow{\ \text{NaOH}(aq),\ \text{heat}\ }$ propan-1-ol
- propan-1-ol $\xrightarrow{\ \text{hot, concentrated KMnO}_4/\text{H}^+(aq)\ }$ Compound B
- propan-1-ol $\xrightarrow{\ \text{concentrated H}_2\text{SO}_4\ }$ Compound C
- Compound C $\xrightarrow{\ \text{H}_2(g),\ \text{Pd or Ni catalyst}\ }$ Compound D

Draw the structural formulae for compounds A, B, C and D.
questions.answer:
- **A:** a 1-halopropane, e.g. 1-bromopropane $\text{CH}_3\text{–CH}_2\text{–CH}_2\text{–Br}$ (substitution of Br by $\text{OH}^-$ gives propan-1-ol; 1-chloropropane is also acceptable).
- **B:** propanoic acid $\text{CH}_3\text{–CH}_2\text{–COOH}$, i.e. $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{C(=O)–OH}$ (a primary alcohol is oxidised fully to the carboxylic acid by hot acidified permanganate).
- **C:** propene $\text{CH}_2\text{=CH–CH}_3$ (dehydration by concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$).
- **D:** propane $\text{CH}_3\text{–CH}_2\text{–CH}_3$ (hydrogenation of the double bond).

In the structural formulae all bonds are drawn, e.g. D is a chain of three C atoms each with H atoms on all remaining bonds (8 H), and B has a $\text{C=O}$ and a $\text{C–O–H}$ on the third carbon.

questions.question:
The flow chart shows reactions of a range of organic compounds, all linked to propan-1-ol, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$:
- Compound A $\xrightarrow{\ \text{NaOH}(aq),\ \text{heat}\ }$ propan-1-ol
- propan-1-ol $\xrightarrow{\ \text{hot, concentrated KMnO}_4/\text{H}^+(aq)\ }$ Compound B
- propan-1-ol $\xrightarrow{\ \text{concentrated H}_2\text{SO}_4\ }$ Compound C
- Compound C $\xrightarrow{\ \text{H}_2(g),\ \text{Pd or Ni catalyst}\ }$ Compound D

Outline a chemical test that could be carried out in a school laboratory to identify compound C (propene, the product of dehydrating propan-1-ol). Include an expected observation.
questions.answer: Bromine water test for an alkene: add a few drops of orange-brown bromine water to a sample of compound C in a test tube (bubble the gas through it) and shake, alongside a control of an alkane. Compound C rapidly **decolourises** the bromine water (orange-brown → colourless) because bromine adds across the C=C double bond ($\text{CH}_2\text{=CHCH}_3 + \text{Br}_2 \rightarrow \text{CH}_2\text{BrCHBrCH}_3$); the alkane does not decolourise it quickly (without UV light).

questions.question:
The effect of concentration on the pH of propanoic acid ($\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{COOH}$) and hydrochloric acid (HCl) solutions is shown in the graph. Both these acids are monoprotic.

Explain the trends in the graph. Include two relevant chemical equations in your answer.
questions.answer:
**Trend 1 — both acids:** pH decreases as concentration increases, because $[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]$ increases.

**Trend 2 — HCl:** pH falls by exactly 1 unit for each tenfold increase in concentration (pH = $-\log[\text{HCl}]$, a straight line from pH 6 at $10^{-6}$ M to pH 1 at $10^{-1}$ M). HCl is a strong acid and ionises completely at all concentrations, so $[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+] = [\text{HCl}]$:

$$\text{HCl}(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightarrow \text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq) + \text{Cl}^-(aq)$$

**Trend 3 — propanoic acid:** at very low concentrations its pH is almost the same as HCl's, but as concentration increases its pH falls less and less (by only about 0.5 per tenfold increase), so the gap from HCl widens. Propanoic acid is a weak acid that ionises only partially in an equilibrium:

$$\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{COOH}(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightleftharpoons \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{COO}^-(aq) + \text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq)$$

When the solution is very dilute, by Le Chatelier's principle (more water, fewer particles) the equilibrium lies further right and the acid is almost fully ionised, so it behaves like HCl. At higher concentrations the percentage ionisation is much lower ($[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+] \approx \sqrt{K_a c}$), so $[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]$ is much less than the acid concentration and the pH is higher than that of HCl of the same concentration.

questions.question:
Lead(II) bromide is a sparingly soluble salt.

$$\text{PbBr}_2(s) \rightleftharpoons \text{Pb}^{2+}(aq) + 2\text{Br}^-(aq) \qquad K_{sp} = 2.1 \times 10^{-6}$$

The table states the molar solubility of lead(II) bromide in water and in various metal bromide solutions of equal concentration at 25°C.

| Solvent | Molar solubility of $\text{PbBr}_2$ in solvent (M) |
|---|---|
| distilled water | $8.1 \times 10^{-3}$ |
| 0.1 M sodium bromide | $2.1 \times 10^{-4}$ |
| 0.1 M aluminium bromide | $2.3 \times 10^{-5}$ |

State the common ion effect.
questions.answer: The common ion effect is the decrease in the solubility of a salt when the solution already contains one of the ions in that salt (a common ion): by Le Chatelier's principle the common ion shifts the dissolution equilibrium towards the solid (precipitation).

questions.question:
Lead(II) bromide is a sparingly soluble salt.

$$\text{PbBr}_2(s) \rightleftharpoons \text{Pb}^{2+}(aq) + 2\text{Br}^-(aq) \qquad K_{sp} = 2.1 \times 10^{-6}$$

The table states the molar solubility of lead(II) bromide in water and in various metal bromide solutions of equal concentration at 25°C.

| Solvent | Molar solubility of $\text{PbBr}_2$ in solvent (M) |
|---|---|
| distilled water | $8.1 \times 10^{-3}$ |
| 0.1 M sodium bromide | $2.1 \times 10^{-4}$ |
| 0.1 M aluminium bromide | $2.3 \times 10^{-5}$ |

Explain the difference in the molar solubility of lead(II) bromide in each of the solvents in the table.
questions.answer:
- **Distilled water** contains no $\text{Br}^-$ (no common ion), so the solubility is highest, $8.1 \times 10^{-3}$ M (consistent with $s = \sqrt[3]{K_{sp}/4}$).
- **0.1 M NaBr** contains 0.1 M $\text{Br}^-$. The added bromide ions shift the equilibrium $\text{PbBr}_2(s) \rightleftharpoons \text{Pb}^{2+}(aq) + 2\text{Br}^-(aq)$ to the left (Le Chatelier's principle: the rate of precipitation increases relative to the rate of dissolution), so less $\text{PbBr}_2$ dissolves: $s = K_{sp}/(0.1)^2 = 2.1 \times 10^{-4}$ M.
- **0.1 M $\text{AlBr}_3$** releases 3 $\text{Br}^-$ per formula unit, so $[\text{Br}^-] = 0.3$ M — three times that in the NaBr solution. The equilibrium is shifted even further left, so solubility is lowest: $s = 2.1 \times 10^{-6}/(0.3)^2 = 2.3 \times 10^{-5}$ M.

So the higher the concentration of the common $\text{Br}^-$ ion, the lower the molar solubility of $\text{PbBr}_2$.

questions.question:
Snow White has noticed that her chickens' eggshells were noticeably thinner and easily cracked in summer. She found out that an average eggshell should contain between 85–93% calcium carbonate. To determine the percentage by mass of calcium carbonate in the eggshells she followed the steps below:

1. The shell was dried in a drying oven for 30 minutes to remove any water.
2. The shell was crushed into powder and the powder was weighed using an electronic balance. The mass of the dried eggshell was 1.25 g.
3. The powdered eggshell was transferred into a 250 mL conical flask.
4. Exactly 25.00 mL of 0.971 mol L$^{-1}$ hydrochloric acid was added to the eggshell in the conical flask until the eggshell was completely dissolved. Three drops of phenolphthalein indicator were added to this solution.
5. A standardised solution of 0.598 mol L$^{-1}$ sodium hydroxide was added to a 50.00 mL burette.
6. The sodium hydroxide was titrated against the solution in the flask once, and the titre value was found to be 12.55 mL.

Calculate the percentage by mass of calcium carbonate in the eggshell AND state whether Snow White has reason to be concerned about her chickens' eggshells.
questions.answer:
Back titration of the excess acid: $\text{HCl}(aq) + \text{NaOH}(aq) \rightarrow \text{NaCl}(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$

$n(\text{NaOH}) = 0.598 \times 0.01255 = 7.505 \times 10^{-3}$ mol $= n(\text{HCl})_\text{excess}$ (1 : 1)

$n(\text{HCl})_\text{initial} = 0.971 \times 0.02500 = 2.4275 \times 10^{-2}$ mol

$n(\text{HCl})_\text{reacted with shell} = 0.024275 - 0.007505 = 1.6770 \times 10^{-2}$ mol

$\text{CaCO}_3(s) + 2\text{HCl}(aq) \rightarrow \text{CaCl}_2(aq) + \text{CO}_2(g) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$, so $n(\text{CaCO}_3) = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 0.016770 = 8.385 \times 10^{-3}$ mol

$M(\text{CaCO}_3) = 40.08 + 12.01 + 3(16.00) = 100.09\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$; $m(\text{CaCO}_3) = 8.385 \times 10^{-3} \times 100.09 = 0.8393$ g

$$\%\,\text{CaCO}_3 = \frac{0.8393}{1.25} \times 100 = 67.1\%$$

67.1% is well below the normal 85–93%, so Snow White does have reason to be concerned about her chickens' eggshells.

questions.question:
Carbon dioxide is produced as a waste product of cellular respiration and leaves the body through exhalation (breathing out). The equations below show the steps in the equilibrium system in chickens:

1. $\text{CO}_2(g)$ (in chicken breath) $\rightleftharpoons \text{CO}_2(aq)$ (in bloodstream)
2. $\text{CO}_2(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightleftharpoons \text{H}_2\text{CO}_3(aq)$
3. $\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3(aq) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{H}^+(aq) + \text{CO}_3^{2-}(aq)$
4. $\text{Ca}^{2+}(aq) + \text{CO}_3^{2-}(aq) \rightleftharpoons \text{CaCO}_3(s)$ (egg shells)

When a chicken gets hot, it does not perspire, but instead it pants like a dog.

Using Le Châtelier's principle and the equations above, explain why chickens lay thin-shelled eggs in hot weather.
questions.answer: In hot weather chickens pant, so they exhale more $\text{CO}_2(g)$, removing it from the system. By Le Châtelier's principle, equilibrium 1 shifts left to partially replace the lost $\text{CO}_2(g)$, lowering $[\text{CO}_2(aq)]$ in the blood. This shifts equilibrium 2 left, lowering $[\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3]$, which shifts equilibrium 3 left, lowering $[\text{CO}_3^{2-}]$. Lower $[\text{CO}_3^{2-}]$ shifts equilibrium 4 left, so less $\text{CaCO}_3(s)$ forms — the eggshells are thinner.

questions.question:
A buffer was made using 50 mL of 0.025 M sodium carbonate solution and 50 mL of 0.025 M sodium hydrogen carbonate solution.

A few drops of universal indicator were added, and the initial colour was observed to be dark blue. Using a probe the pH was determined to be 10.0.

When 1 mL of 0.10 M NaOH(aq) was added, no change in the colour of the solution was observed.

Explain the observations of the colour of the indicator before and after the addition of NaOH(aq). Support your answer with at least ONE chemical equation.
questions.answer:
The solution is a buffer: it contains equal amounts of a weak Brønsted–Lowry acid, $\text{HCO}_3^-$, and its conjugate base, $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$, in equilibrium:

$$\text{CO}_3^{2-}(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightleftharpoons \text{HCO}_3^-(aq) + \text{OH}^-(aq)$$

**Before:** the hydrolysis of carbonate produces enough $\text{OH}^-$ to make the solution basic (pH 10.0), so universal indicator is dark blue.

**After adding NaOH:** the added $\text{OH}^-$ increases $[\text{OH}^-]$. By Le Chatelier's principle the equilibrium shifts left to counteract this: the large reservoir of $\text{HCO}_3^-$ reacts with the added hydroxide,

$$\text{HCO}_3^-(aq) + \text{OH}^-(aq) \rightarrow \text{CO}_3^{2-}(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$$

Because only a small amount of $\text{OH}^-$ ($1 \times 10^{-4}$ mol) was added compared with the $1.25 \times 10^{-3}$ mol of $\text{HCO}_3^-$ present, almost all of it is removed and the ratio $[\text{CO}_3^{2-}]/[\text{HCO}_3^-]$ hardly changes. The pH stays at about 10, so the indicator remains dark blue.

questions.question:
Aurora wished to make an acidic buffer using acetic acid and sodium acetate. She started with 100 mL of 0.100 M acetic acid in a conical flask.

The $K_a$ for acetic acid is $1.76 \times 10^{-5}$ and the pH of the buffer solution is 5.00.

$$\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightleftharpoons \text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-(aq) + \text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq)$$

Calculate the mass of sodium acetate which should be added to the flask by Aurora to prepare the acidic buffer.
questions.answer:
$\text{pH} = 5.00 \Rightarrow [\text{H}_3\text{O}^+] = 1.0 \times 10^{-5}$ M.

$$K_a = \frac{[\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-][\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]}{[\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}]}$$

In a buffer $[\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-] \ne [\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]$; the acetate comes from the added salt and $[\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}] \approx 0.100$ M (its ionisation is negligible). So

$$[\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-] = \frac{K_a[\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}]}{[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]} = \frac{1.76 \times 10^{-5} \times 0.100}{1.0 \times 10^{-5}} = 0.176\ \text{M}$$

$n(\text{CH}_3\text{COONa}) = 0.176 \times 0.100 = 0.0176$ mol

$M(\text{CH}_3\text{COONa}) = 22.99 + 2(12.01) + 2(16.00) + 3(1.008) = 82.03\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$

$m = 0.0176 \times 82.03 = 1.44$ g of sodium acetate (assuming no volume change).

questions.question:
A partially labelled bottle was found in the chemical storeroom. The label indicated that the compound, **Compound X**, was flammable.

Cinderella carried out an oxidation reaction on Compound X and then had some spectroscopic testing completed on the product. From the spectroscopic testing the product of the oxidation reaction was identified as a ketone, 3-methylbutan-2-one, $\text{CH}_3\text{–CO–CH(CH}_3)\text{–CH}_3$:

$$\text{Compound X} \xrightarrow{\ [\text{O}]\ } \text{3-methylbutan-2-one}$$

The IR spectrum (Figure 1) and $^{13}$C NMR spectrum (Figure 2) of the product, 3-methylbutan-2-one, are shown. The IR spectrum has a strong C–H absorption near 2900–3000 cm$^{-1}$ and a strong sharp peak near 1715 cm$^{-1}$; the $^{13}$C NMR spectrum has peaks at about 212, 42, 27 and 18 ppm.

- Draw and name Compound X.
- Describe (or sketch) the peaks you would expect in the IR spectrum of Compound X in the region 4000–1600 cm$^{-1}$, and the approximate locations of the peaks in its $^{13}$C NMR spectrum.
- For both the IR spectrum and the $^{13}$C NMR spectrum of Compound X, justify one similarity and one difference when compared to 3-methylbutan-2-one.
questions.answer:
**Compound X** is the secondary alcohol that oxidises to this ketone: **3-methylbutan-2-ol**, $\text{CH}_3\text{–CH(OH)–CH(CH}_3)\text{–CH}_3$ (a four-carbon chain with $-\text{OH}$ on C2 and $-\text{CH}_3$ on C3; all other bonds to H).

**Expected IR spectrum of X (4000–1600 cm$^{-1}$):** a strong, broad O–H (alcohol) peak centred around 3200–3550 cm$^{-1}$, plus sharp C–H (sp$^3$) peaks just below 3000 cm$^{-1}$ (2850–3000 cm$^{-1}$); no peak near 1700 cm$^{-1}$.

**Expected $^{13}$C NMR of X:** 4 peaks — one at about 70–75 ppm (the C–OH carbon) and three in the 15–40 ppm region (the CH carbon at about 35 ppm and the methyl carbons at about 18–20 ppm).

| Spectrum | Similarity | Difference |
|---|---|---|
| IR | Both show C–H stretching peaks at about 2850–3000 cm$^{-1}$, because both molecules contain sp$^3$ C–H bonds in the same carbon skeleton. | The ketone has a strong sharp C=O peak at about 1715 cm$^{-1}$, which X lacks; X instead has a broad O–H peak at about 3200–3550 cm$^{-1}$ (hydrogen-bonded alcohol), which the ketone lacks. |
| $^{13}$C NMR | Both have 5 carbons but only 4 carbon environments (the two methyls on C3 are equivalent), so both show 4 peaks; both have one peak well downfield (C bonded to O) and three upfield peaks (10–45 ppm) from the alkyl carbons. | The ketone's C=O carbon appears at about 210 ppm, whereas X's C–OH carbon is less deshielded and appears at only about 70 ppm. |

*Note:* the paper's sample answer places the C–OH carbon "around 90 ppm"; the expected value (and the paper's own marking criteria) is about 70 ppm (alcohol C–O: 50–90 ppm range, ≈73 ppm for this alcohol).

questions.question:
27.62 g of hydrated sodium carbonate crystals, $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3 \cdot x\text{H}_2\text{O}(s)$, was dissolved in water and made up to 1.000 L. 25.00 mL of this solution was neutralised by 24.13 mL of hydrochloric acid of concentration 0.2000 M.

Write an equation for the reaction between sodium carbonate solution and hydrochloric acid.
questions.answer: $$\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3(aq) + 2\text{HCl}(aq) \rightarrow 2\text{NaCl}(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) + \text{CO}_2(g)$$

questions.question:
27.62 g of hydrated sodium carbonate crystals, $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3 \cdot x\text{H}_2\text{O}(s)$, was dissolved in water and made up to 1.000 L. 25.00 mL of this solution was neutralised by 24.13 mL of hydrochloric acid of concentration 0.2000 M.

Calculate the molar concentration of the sodium carbonate solution neutralised by the hydrochloric acid.
questions.answer:
$n(\text{HCl}) = 0.2000 \times 0.02413 = 4.826 \times 10^{-3}$ mol

From $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3 + 2\text{HCl} \rightarrow \dots$: $n(\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3) = \tfrac12 \times 4.826 \times 10^{-3} = 2.413 \times 10^{-3}$ mol

$$c(\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3) = \frac{2.413 \times 10^{-3}}{0.02500} = 0.09652\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$$

questions.question:
27.62 g of hydrated sodium carbonate crystals, $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3 \cdot x\text{H}_2\text{O}(s)$, was dissolved in water and made up to 1.000 L. 25.00 mL of this solution was neutralised by 24.13 mL of hydrochloric acid of concentration 0.2000 M.

The concentration of the sodium carbonate solution was found to be 0.09652 mol L$^{-1}$. By calculating the mass of water in the hydrated crystals, find the value of $x$.

Elsa carried out an experiment to compare the energy changes when solid ionic compounds dissolve in water and to compare their Gibbs free energy. She observed that the temperature of the solution fell when potassium chloride dissolved but rose when sodium hydroxide dissolved.

Elsa correctly concluded: *"The dissolution of both potassium chloride and of sodium hydroxide occur spontaneously."*

Justify the conclusion made by Elsa by referring to the changes in enthalpy, entropy and Gibbs free energy.
questions.answer:
A process is spontaneous when $\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S < 0$.

**Entropy (both):** when an ionic solid dissolves, the ordered lattice breaks up into freely moving hydrated ions spread through the solution, so disorder increases: $\Delta S > 0$ for both, and $-T\Delta S$ is negative.

**KCl:** the temperature fell, so heat was absorbed from the surroundings — dissolution is endothermic, $\Delta H > 0$. Since KCl dissolved by itself, the entropy term must outweigh the enthalpy term ($T\Delta S > \Delta H$), so $\Delta G < 0$: the dissolution is entropy-driven and spontaneous.

**NaOH:** the temperature rose, so dissolution is exothermic, $\Delta H < 0$. With $\Delta H < 0$ and $\Delta S > 0$, $\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$ is negative at all temperatures, so the dissolution is spontaneous.

Since $\Delta G < 0$ for both, both dissolve spontaneously, which justifies Elsa's conclusion.

questions.question:
Biofuels are becoming an increasingly important alternative to fossil fuels worldwide. However, biofuel production and consumption in Australia remained low in 2022.

The following data provides a comparison of the properties of petrol and bioethanol (Thakur & Kaviti, 2018).

| Property | Petrol | Bioethanol |
|---|---|---|
| Chemical formula | C$_5$ – C$_{12}$ | $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}$ |
| C : O : H fractions (mass %) | 87.4 : 0 : 12.6 | 52.2 : 34.7 : 13.0 |
| Stoichiometric air–fuel ratio | 14.2 – 15.1 | 8.97 |
| Octane rating | 91 – 100 | 108.61 – 110 |
| Heat of combustion (kJ mol$^{-1}$) | 5460 | 1370 |
| Density at 15°C (g mL$^{-1}$) | 0.750 | 0.785 |
| Solubility in water (%) | 0 | 100 |
| Average cost of production (AUD per litre of gasoline equivalent, LGE) | 1.17 | 1.50 |

Assess the potential of ethanol as an alternative fuel and discuss the advantages and disadvantages to support its future increased use in Australia.

Include balanced chemical equations for both the production and use of ethanol and refer to the data provided in your answer.
questions.answer:
**Production.** Bioethanol is made by fermenting glucose from biomass (e.g. sugar cane, grain, or cellulose broken down to glucose) with yeast under anaerobic conditions at about 37°C:

$$\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6(aq) \xrightarrow{\ \text{yeast}\ } 2\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}(aq) + 2\text{CO}_2(g)$$

followed by distillation to concentrate the ethanol.

**Use.** Ethanol burns cleanly in air:

$$\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}(l) + 3\text{O}_2(g) \rightarrow 2\text{CO}_2(g) + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$$

**Advantages**
- *Renewable:* it is made from crops that can be regrown, unlike petrol from finite crude oil, and local production would reduce Australia's dependence on imported fuel.
- *Lower net CO$_2$:* the $\text{CO}_2$ released on combustion was absorbed by photosynthesis while the crop grew, so in principle it is closer to carbon neutral.
- *Cleaner combustion:* ethanol contains 34.7% oxygen by mass (petrol 0%) and needs a lower air–fuel ratio (8.97 vs 14.2–15.1), so it combusts more completely, producing less CO and soot.
- *Higher octane rating* (108.6–110 vs 91–100), so it resists knocking and can replace toxic octane-boosting additives; it can be blended with petrol (e.g. E10) in existing engines.
- *Spills:* being 100% water-soluble and biodegradable, spills dilute and break down quickly.

**Disadvantages**
- *Lower energy content:* per gram, ethanol releases $1370/46.07 \approx 29.7$ kJ g$^{-1}$ compared with about $5460/114.2 \approx 47.8$ kJ g$^{-1}$ for octane; with similar densities (0.785 vs 0.750 g mL$^{-1}$) a car needs about 1.5 times the volume of ethanol to travel the same distance.
- *Higher cost:* production costs \$1.50 per LGE compared with \$1.17 for petrol, largely because of the energy needed for distillation and dehydration.
- *Not truly carbon neutral:* fossil fuels are used to grow, fertilise and harvest crops, transport them and distil the ethanol, and fermentation itself releases $\text{CO}_2$.
- *Land and water use:* large areas of arable land and lots of water are needed — competing with food production in a dry country like Australia.
- *Engine and handling issues:* ethanol absorbs water (100% miscible), which can corrode metal parts and damage rubber seals; high blends need modified engines, and spills cannot be skimmed off water.

**Assessment.** Ethanol has real potential as a renewable, cleaner-burning, high-octane fuel, but its lower energy per litre, higher cost and the land, water and energy required to produce it mean it cannot replace petrol completely in the near future. The best path for Australia is an increased use of ethanol–petrol blends (E10, and E85 for suitable vehicles), especially if it is produced from waste biomass (e.g. sugar-cane bagasse and cellulosic waste) so it does not compete with food crops and its production costs fall.

*Note:* the paper's table gives the densities in g L$^{-1}$; the values 0.750 and 0.785 are in g mL$^{-1}$ (kg L$^{-1}$).

questions.question: What is the measurement taken by an atomic absorption spectrometer?
questions.answer: An AAS passes light of a wavelength specific to the element through the atomised sample and measures how much is absorbed (the absorbance), which is proportional to concentration.

questions.question:
Ammonia is produced in the Haber process in the following reaction.

$$\text{N}_2(g) + 3\text{H}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NH}_3(g)$$

Magnetite (an iron oxide) is a commonly used catalyst for this reaction. In an industrial setting, what will be the effect of magnetite on the equilibrium concentration of hydrogen gas?
options: A decrease in the rate of reaction
An increase in the rate of reaction
No effect on the concentration of hydrogen gas
A decrease in the concentration of hydrogen gas
questions.answer:
A catalyst lowers the activation energy of the forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached faster but the position of equilibrium (and so the equilibrium $[\text{H}_2]$) is unchanged. A and B describe rates, not the equilibrium concentration.

*(Note: the paper gave magnetite's formula as $\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3$; magnetite is $\text{Fe}_3\text{O}_4$.)*

questions.question:
The equilibrium constant for the reaction $\text{Br}_2(g) + \text{I}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{IBr}(g)$ is $K_{eq} = 1.2 \times 10^{2}$ at $150^\circ\text{C}$.

What is $K_{eq}$ for the reaction $4\text{IBr}(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{Br}_2(g) + 2\text{I}_2(g)$ at $150^\circ\text{C}$?
questions.answer: Reversing the reaction inverts $K$, and doubling the coefficients squares it: $K' = \left(\dfrac{1}{1.2 \times 10^{2}}\right)^2 = \dfrac{1}{14400} = 6.9 \times 10^{-5}$.

questions.question:
The four equations below represent different equilibrium systems.

| | Equation | $\Delta H$ |
|---|---|---|
| Equation 1 | $2\text{SO}_2(g) + \text{O}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{SO}_3(g)$ | $-180\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ |
| Equation 2 | $\text{CO}(g) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{CO}_2(g) + \text{H}_2(g)$ | $-46\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ |
| Equation 3 | $\text{PCl}_5(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{PCl}_3(g) + \text{Cl}_2(g)$ | $+93\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ |
| Equation 4 | $\text{CH}_4(g) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{CO}(g) + 3\text{H}_2(g)$ | $+205\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ |

After equilibrium was established in each system, the temperature was decreased and the pressure was increased.

In which equilibrium system would both changes result in an increase in yield?
questions.answer: Decreasing temperature favours the exothermic forward reaction (equations 1 and 2); increasing pressure favours the side with fewer moles of gas (equation 1: 3 mol $\rightarrow$ 2 mol; equation 2 has equal moles). Only equation 1 benefits from both.

questions.question: Which reagents and conditions are best for converting propan-1-ol into propanoic acid?
questions.answer: A primary alcohol is oxidised to a carboxylic acid by heating (under reflux) with an oxidising agent such as acidified $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$. Concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ alone would dehydrate it to propene.

questions.question: A solution was prepared by dissolving 70 g of $\text{KNO}_3$ in 200 mL of water at $60^\circ\text{C}$. The solution was cooled to $10^\circ\text{C}$. Using the solubility curves shown, how much $\text{KNO}_3$ will be deposited as a solid?
questions.answer: From the curve, the solubility of $\text{KNO}_3$ at $10^\circ\text{C}$ is about 20 g per 100 g water, so 200 g of water holds about 40 g. Mass deposited $= 70 - 40 = 30$ g.

questions.question: If Solution X has a pH of 3 and Solution Y has a pH of 6, we can conclude that:
options: $[\text{H}^+]$ in Solution X is half that of $[\text{H}^+]$ in Solution Y
$[\text{OH}^-]$ in Solution Y is twice that of $[\text{OH}^-]$ in Solution X
Solution Y must contain a stronger acid than Solution X
$[\text{H}^+]$ in Solution X is 1000 times that of $[\text{H}^+]$ in Solution Y
questions.answer: $[\text{H}^+] = 10^{-\text{pH}}$: $10^{-3}/10^{-6} = 1000$. pH alone says nothing about acid strength (C).

questions.question: The diagram below represents a titration curve for the reaction between a particular acid and a particular base. Which of these equations best represents the reaction described in the titration curve?
questions.answer: The starting pH (about 10.5) shows a weak base, the final pH (about 2) shows a strong acid is being added, and the equivalence point is below 7 (about 5) — the profile of a strong acid/weak base titration: HCl with $\text{NH}_3$.

questions.question: What volume of 0.25 mol/L hydrochloric acid is required to react completely with 40 mL of 0.50 mol/L calcium hydroxide?
questions.answer: $\text{Ca(OH)}_2 + 2\text{HCl} \rightarrow \text{CaCl}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$. $n(\text{Ca(OH)}_2) = 0.50 \times 0.040 = 0.020$ mol, so $n(\text{HCl}) = 0.040$ mol and $V = 0.040/0.25 = 0.160$ L $= 160$ mL.

questions.question: Which one of the following represents a conjugate acid-base pair?
questions.answer: A conjugate pair differs by exactly one $\text{H}^+$: $\text{NH}_3 \rightarrow \text{NH}_2^- + \text{H}^+$. C differs by three protons.

questions.question: Which statement accurately describes the equivalence point in an acid-base titration?
options: The pH of the solution is 7
The volume of acid equals the volume of base
The mole ratio of acid to base is equal to the stoichiometric ratio
questions.answer: At the equivalence point the acid and base have been added in exactly the stoichiometric mole ratio. The indicator colour change marks the end point (which may differ), and the pH is 7 only for strong acid/strong base titrations.

questions.question: One litre of an aqueous solution of potassium hydroxide has a pH of 12.0 at $25^\circ\text{C}$. How many moles of solid potassium hydroxide must be added to raise the pH to 13.0?
questions.answer: pH 12 $\Rightarrow$ pOH 2, $[\text{OH}^-] = 0.010$ mol/L; pH 13 $\Rightarrow$ $[\text{OH}^-] = 0.10$ mol/L. In 1 L, $0.10 - 0.010 = 0.09$ mol KOH must be added.

questions.question: $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ and $\text{HNO}_3$ are both strong acids. $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ is a weak acid. 20.00 mL solutions of 0.10 mol/L concentrations of each of these acids were separately titrated with a 0.10 mol/L solution of NaOH. In order to react completely:
options: all three acids will require the same amount of NaOH
$\text{HNO}_3$ will require more NaOH than $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ but less than $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$
$\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ and $\text{HNO}_3$ will require the same amount of NaOH but $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ will require less
$\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ and $\text{HNO}_3$ will require the same amount of NaOH but $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ will require more
questions.answer: The amount of base needed depends on the moles of acidic protons, not acid strength. $\text{HNO}_3$ and $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ are both monoprotic (0.0020 mol NaOH each); diprotic $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ needs twice as much.

questions.question: What is produced when 1-chlorobutane is treated with aqueous sodium hydroxide solution?
questions.answer: Substitution: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Cl} + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH} + \text{Cl}^-$, giving butan-1-ol.

questions.question: Which compound produces this mass spectrum?
questions.answer: The molecular ion is at $m/z = 60$, which rules out ethane-1,2-diol (62) and chloroethane (64/66). Ethanoic acid (60) fits the fragments: 45 is $[\text{COOH}]^+$ (loss of $\text{CH}_3$, 15) and the base peak 43 is $[\text{CH}_3\text{CO}]^+$ (loss of OH, 17), with 15 for $[\text{CH}_3]^+$.

questions.question: What is the IUPAC name of the molecule shown?
questions.answer: The longest chain runs through the ethyl group: 6 carbons (hexane). Numbering from the end nearest a branch puts methyl groups on C2 and C4: 2,4-dimethylhexane.

questions.question: What is the ratio of areas under each signal in the $^1$H NMR spectrum of 2-methylbutane?
questions.answer: 2-methylbutane is $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CH}\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$: four H environments — the two equivalent $\text{CH}_3$ groups (6H), the CH (1H), the $\text{CH}_2$ (2H) and the end $\text{CH}_3$ (3H), giving 6 : 1 : 2 : 3.

questions.question: Which monomer forms the polymer shown?
questions.answer: The repeating two-carbon unit is $-\text{CH(Cl)}-\text{CH(CH}_3)-$, so the addition monomer has a C=C bond between a carbon bearing H and Cl and a carbon bearing H and $\text{CH}_3$: $\text{CHCl=CHCH}_3$ (1-chloropropene).

questions.question: Cellulose is a condensation polymer formed from the glucose monomer $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6$. What would be the molar mass of a cellulose polymer made from 125 monomer units?
questions.answer: $M(\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6) = 180.156$ g/mol. Joining 125 units releases 124 water molecules: $125 \times 180.156 - 124 \times 18.016 = 22519.5 - 2234.0 = 20285.5$ g/mol.

questions.question:
$\text{NO}_2$ reacts to form $\text{N}_2\text{O}_4$ as follows:

$$2\text{NO}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{N}_2\text{O}_4(g) \qquad \Delta H = -57.2\ \text{kJ/mol}$$

Outline what happens to the enthalpy ($H$) and entropy ($S$) as this system is cooled.
questions.answer:
**Enthalpy:** the forward reaction is exothermic, so cooling shifts the equilibrium to the right (Le Chatelier's principle). As more $\text{N}_2\text{O}_4$ forms, heat is released to the surroundings, so the enthalpy of the system decreases (the value of $\Delta H$ for the reaction, $-57.2$ kJ/mol, stays essentially constant).

**Entropy:** the entropy of the system decreases. The shift to the right converts 2 mol of gas into 1 mol of gas (fewer particles, fewer possible arrangements), and the lower temperature also reduces molecular motion, decreasing the number of accessible microstates.

questions.question: Qualitatively compare the solubility of lead(II) chloride in water with its solubility in a solution of sodium chloride. Include an equation in your answer.
questions.answer:
Lead(II) chloride is less soluble in sodium chloride solution than in pure water.

$$\text{PbCl}_2(s) \rightleftharpoons \text{Pb}^{2+}(aq) + 2\text{Cl}^-(aq)$$

This is the common ion effect. The NaCl solution already contains $\text{Cl}^-$ ions, so the ionic product $[\text{Pb}^{2+}][\text{Cl}^-]^2$ reaches $K_{sp}$ when much less $\text{PbCl}_2$ has dissolved. Equivalently, by Le Chatelier's principle the high $[\text{Cl}^-]$ shifts the equilibrium to the left, favouring the solid, so less $\text{PbCl}_2$ dissolves.

questions.question:
The concentration–time graph below is for the following reaction system:

$$\text{CO}(g) + \text{Cl}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{COCl}_2(g) \qquad \Delta H = -220\ \text{kJ/mol}$$

At time = 0 seconds, there was no CO gas present in the system. (The three curves are not labelled: blue starts at 0 and levels off at 0.5 mol/L; orange starts at 0.3 and levels off at 0.8 mol/L; grey starts at 0.7 and levels off at 0.2 mol/L.)

Calculate the equilibrium constant at 40 seconds.
questions.answer:
Since no CO was present at $t = 0$, the curve starting at 0 (blue) is CO, so the system reached equilibrium by $\text{COCl}_2$ decomposing. The grey curve falls by 0.5 mol/L while the orange rises by 0.5 mol/L (1 : 1 ratio), so grey is $\text{COCl}_2$ and orange is $\text{Cl}_2$.

At 40 s: $[\text{CO}] = 0.5$, $[\text{Cl}_2] = 0.8$, $[\text{COCl}_2] = 0.2$ mol/L.

$$K_{eq} = \frac{[\text{COCl}_2]}{[\text{CO}][\text{Cl}_2]} = \frac{0.2}{0.5 \times 0.8} = 0.5$$

questions.question:
The concentration–time graph below is for the following reaction system:

$$\text{CO}(g) + \text{Cl}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{COCl}_2(g) \qquad \Delta H = -220\ \text{kJ/mol}$$

At time = 0 seconds, there was no CO gas present in the system. (The three curves are not labelled: blue starts at 0 and levels off at 0.5 mol/L; orange starts at 0.3 and levels off at 0.8 mol/L; grey starts at 0.7 and levels off at 0.2 mol/L.)

At 50 seconds the volume of the system was halved, keeping the temperature constant. Sketch how the graph continues after 50 s, showing how this change would affect the reaction system and how the system would respond until equilibrium is restored.
questions.answer:
- **At 50 s:** halving the volume instantly doubles every concentration: $[\text{CO}]$ $0.5 \rightarrow 1.0$, $[\text{Cl}_2]$ $0.8 \rightarrow 1.6$, $[\text{COCl}_2]$ $0.2 \rightarrow 0.4$ mol/L (vertical jumps).
- **Response:** the increased pressure is partially counteracted by a shift to the side with fewer gas moles (the right). $[\text{COCl}_2]$ then rises gradually while $[\text{CO}]$ and $[\text{Cl}_2]$ fall gradually, all changing by equal amounts (1 : 1 : 1 mole ratio), before levelling off.
- **New equilibrium:** $K_{eq}$ is unchanged (0.5) since temperature is constant. Solving $\dfrac{0.4 + x}{(1.0 - x)(1.6 - x)} = 0.5$ gives $x \approx 0.18$, so the curves level off at about $[\text{CO}] = 0.82$, $[\text{Cl}_2] = 1.42$ and $[\text{COCl}_2] = 0.58$ mol/L.

questions.question:
Water gas, a mixture of carbon monoxide, hydrogen and oxygen, can react in the following exothermic reaction.

$$\text{H}_2(g) + \text{CO}(g) + \text{O}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{CO}_2(g) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(g)$$

Use collision theory to explain how the following change would affect this equilibrium: a decrease in temperature.
questions.answer: Decreasing the temperature lowers the average kinetic energy of the molecules, so a smaller fraction of collisions have energy equal to or greater than the activation energy, and the rates of both the forward and reverse reactions decrease. Because the forward reaction is exothermic, the reverse (endothermic) reaction has the higher activation energy, so its rate decreases by a greater proportion. The forward rate is temporarily greater than the reverse rate, so the equilibrium shifts to the right (more $\text{CO}_2$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$) until the rates become equal again.

questions.question:
Water gas, a mixture of carbon monoxide, hydrogen and oxygen, can react in the following exothermic reaction.

$$\text{H}_2(g) + \text{CO}(g) + \text{O}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{CO}_2(g) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(g)$$

Use collision theory to explain how the following change would affect this equilibrium: a decrease in the pressure.
questions.answer: Decreasing the pressure (by increasing the volume) lowers the concentration of every gas, so the collision frequency and the rates of both reactions fall. The forward reaction requires collisions between three reactant particles (3 mol of gas) while the reverse requires only two (2 mol of gas), so the forward rate decreases more than the reverse rate. The reverse rate is temporarily greater, so the equilibrium shifts to the left (towards $\text{H}_2$, CO and $\text{O}_2$) until the rates are equal again.

questions.question: Formic acid ($\text{HCO}_2\text{H}$) has a p$K_a$ of 3.77. Calculate the pH of a 0.250 mol/L solution of this acid.
questions.answer:
$K_a = 10^{-3.77} = 1.698 \times 10^{-4}$

$$\text{HCO}_2\text{H}(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightleftharpoons \text{HCO}_2^-(aq) + \text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq)$$

$$K_a = \frac{[\text{HCO}_2^-][\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]}{[\text{HCO}_2\text{H}]} = \frac{x^2}{0.250 - x} \approx \frac{x^2}{0.250}$$

(assuming $x$ is negligible compared with 0.250, since the acid is weak).

$x^2 = 1.698 \times 10^{-4} \times 0.250 = 4.245 \times 10^{-5}$, so $x = [\text{H}_3\text{O}^+] = 6.52 \times 10^{-3}$ mol/L

$\text{pH} = -\log_{10}(6.52 \times 10^{-3}) = 2.19$

(Check: $x$ is 2.6% of 0.250, so the approximation is valid.)

questions.question: Glycolic acid, $\text{CH}_2(\text{OH})\text{COOH}$, is used in some skincare products. Draw the structural formula of glycolic acid.
questions.answer: A central carbon bonded to two H atoms and an –OH group, joined to a carboxyl group: $\text{HO–CH}_2\text{–C(=O)–OH}$ (all bonds and atoms shown in a full structural formula).

questions.question:
Glycolic acid, $\text{CH}_2(\text{OH})\text{COOH}$, ionises in water as follows:

$$\text{CH}_2(\text{OH})\text{COOH}(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightleftharpoons \text{CH}_2(\text{OH})\text{COO}^-(aq) + \text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq) \qquad K_a = 1.48 \times 10^{-4}$$

Sodium glycolate, $\text{CH}_2(\text{OH})\text{COONa}$, is a soluble salt of glycolic acid.

How does the pH of a solution of glycolic acid change when some solid sodium glycolate is dissolved in the solution? Justify your answer.
questions.answer: The pH increases. Sodium glycolate dissolves completely, increasing $[\text{CH}_2(\text{OH})\text{COO}^-]$ (a product of the equilibrium — a common ion). By Le Chatelier's principle the equilibrium shifts to the left to partially counteract this, consuming $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$. The lower $[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]$ means a higher pH.

questions.question:
100 mL of a 1.00 mol/L solution of glycolic acid, $\text{CH}_2(\text{OH})\text{COOH}$, is spilt on the floor. This could be neutralised by sodium carbonate. The equation for this reaction is shown below:

$$\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3(s) + 2\text{CH}_2(\text{OH})\text{COOH}(aq) \rightarrow 2\text{CH}_2(\text{OH})\text{COONa}(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) + \text{CO}_2(g)$$

What is the minimum mass of sodium carbonate that should be used to neutralise the spill?

A buffer of carbonate ($\text{CO}_3^{2-}$)/hydrogencarbonate ($\text{HCO}_3^-$) is present in blood plasma to maintain a pH between 7.35 and 7.45. Write an equation to show the relevant species in this buffer solution.
questions.answer: $$\text{HCO}_3^-(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightleftharpoons \text{CO}_3^{2-}(aq) + \text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq)$$

questions.question:
Using the carbonate/hydrogencarbonate equilibrium

$$\text{HCO}_3^-(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightleftharpoons \text{CO}_3^{2-}(aq) + \text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq),$$

explain why 300.0 mL of 1.00 mol/L carbonate/hydrogencarbonate buffer does not change in pH significantly when 3 drops of 1.00 mol/L HCl are added to it, yet when 3 drops of 1.00 mol/L HCl are added to 300.0 mL of distilled water there is a significant change in pH.
questions.answer:
**Water:** HCl ionises completely, $\text{HCl}(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightarrow \text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq) + \text{Cl}^-(aq)$. Water has nothing to react with the added $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$, so $[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]$ rises from $10^{-7}$ mol/L to about $5 \times 10^{-4}$ mol/L (3 drops $\approx$ 0.15 mL, $1.5 \times 10^{-4}$ mol in 0.3 L) and the pH drops from 7 to about 3.3.

**Buffer:** the buffer contains large, similar amounts of the weak acid $\text{HCO}_3^-$ and its conjugate base $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$. The added $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ reacts with $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$: $\text{CO}_3^{2-} + \text{H}_3\text{O}^+ \rightarrow \text{HCO}_3^- + \text{H}_2\text{O}$ (the equilibrium shifts to the left). Because the amount of $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$ (about 0.3 mol) is very large compared with the added acid ($\sim 10^{-4}$ mol), almost all the added $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ is removed and the ratio $[\text{CO}_3^{2-}]/[\text{HCO}_3^-]$ is almost unchanged, so the pH barely changes.

questions.question: In a beaker, 12.00 mL of 0.033 mol/L sulfuric acid solution is added to 32.50 mL of 0.0288 mol/L potassium hydroxide solution. Calculate the pH of the resulting solution.

An organic compound, **A** (but-3-en-1-ol, $\text{CH}_2\text{=CHCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$), reacts with ethanoic acid to produce **B** and water, using concentrated sulfuric acid as a catalyst.

Draw the structural formula of **B**.
questions.answer: **B** is the ester but-3-enyl ethanoate, $\text{CH}_3\text{COOCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH=CH}_2$: the C=O of the ethanoate group is bonded through the ester oxygen to the $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH=CH}_2$ chain from the alcohol.

questions.question:
An organic compound, **A** (but-3-en-1-ol, $\text{CH}_2\text{=CHCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$), reacts with ethanoic acid to produce **B** and water, using concentrated sulfuric acid as a catalyst.

Justify, with reference to Le Châtelier's principle, a method to increase the amount of compound **B** produced.
questions.answer: Use an excess of one reactant (e.g. excess ethanoic acid), or remove a product (e.g. remove water, or distil off the ester) as it forms. Esterification is an equilibrium, $\text{A} + \text{CH}_3\text{COOH} \rightleftharpoons \text{B} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$; by Le Châtelier's principle, increasing a reactant concentration (or decreasing a product concentration) shifts the equilibrium to the right to partially counteract the change, increasing the yield of **B**. (Temperature is not a reliable method since $\Delta H$ is not given, and pressure has no effect as the reaction occurs in the liquid phase.) The concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ also absorbs water, which helps shift the equilibrium right.

questions.question:
An organic compound, **A** (but-3-en-1-ol, $\text{CH}_2\text{=CHCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$), reacts with ethanoic acid to produce **B** and water, using concentrated sulfuric acid as a catalyst.

Explain, with reference to intermolecular forces, why compound **B** is more volatile than **A**.
questions.answer: **A** is an alcohol: its –OH group allows strong hydrogen bonding between molecules, in addition to dispersion forces and dipole–dipole forces. **B** is an ester: it has no H atom bonded to O, so it cannot hydrogen bond with other ester molecules — its intermolecular forces are only dispersion forces and weaker dipole–dipole forces (from the polar C=O and C–O bonds). Although **B** is a larger molecule with somewhat stronger dispersion forces, the absence of hydrogen bonding means less energy is needed to separate its molecules, so **B** is more volatile.

questions.question:
An organic compound, **A** (but-3-en-1-ol, $\text{CH}_2\text{=CHCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$), reacts with ethanoic acid to produce **B** and water, using concentrated sulfuric acid as a catalyst.

Justify safety procedures that are needed in carrying out this reaction in a school science laboratory.
questions.answer:
- **No naked flames:** the alcohol, the ester and their vapours are flammable, so heat with an electric heating mantle or water bath rather than a Bunsen burner.
- **Safety glasses and gloves:** concentrated sulfuric acid is highly corrosive and a strong dehydrating agent, and ethanoic acid is corrosive; eye protection and gloves prevent burns from splashes.
- **Fume hood / good ventilation:** the vapours of ethanoic acid, the alcohol and the ester are irritants and flammable, so the reaction should be done in a fume cupboard.
- **Reflux with a condenser (and boiling chips):** heating under reflux stops volatile, flammable vapours escaping into the room, and boiling chips prevent violent bumping of the hot mixture.
- **Dispose of organic waste correctly:** organic liquids go into a labelled organic waste container, not down the sink.

questions.question: Describe two limitations of the Arrhenius theory of acids and bases and how the Brønsted–Lowry model overcomes these limitations.
questions.answer:
Arrhenius defined acids as substances that ionise in water to produce $\text{H}^+$ ions and bases as substances that produce $\text{OH}^-$ ions in water.

1. **Bases without $\text{OH}^-$:** Arrhenius could not explain why substances such as $\text{NH}_3$ or $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$, which contain no hydroxide, are basic. Brønsted–Lowry defines a base as a proton ($\text{H}^+$) acceptor, so $\text{NH}_3$ is a base: $\text{NH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{NH}_4^+ + \text{OH}^-$.
2. **Role of the solvent / non-aqueous reactions:** Arrhenius theory only applies in aqueous solution and ignores the role of water. Brønsted–Lowry treats acid–base reactions as proton transfer, so it includes water's role (acting as a base, forming $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$) and explains reactions with no water, e.g. $\text{HCl}(g) + \text{NH}_3(g) \rightarrow \text{NH}_4\text{Cl}(s)$.

(Other accepted limitation: Arrhenius cannot explain the acidity/basicity of salt solutions such as $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$ or $\text{CH}_3\text{COONa}$, which Brønsted–Lowry explains through conjugate acids and bases.)

questions.question: Combustion analysis of an unknown organic compound indicated that it contained only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. Deduce the identity of the unknown compound using the mass spectrum, infrared spectrum and $^1$H NMR spectrum shown.
questions.answer:
The compound is **propanone**, $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3$ (structural formula: a central C=O carbon bonded to two $\text{CH}_3$ groups).

- **Mass spectrum:** the molecular ion peak at $m/z = 58$ gives a molar mass of 58, which fits $\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\text{O}$. The base peak at 43 is $[\text{CH}_3\text{CO}]^+$ (loss of $\text{CH}_3$, 15) and the peak at 15 is $[\text{CH}_3]^+$.
- **IR spectrum:** the strong, sharp absorption A at about $1700\ \text{cm}^{-1}$ indicates a C=O group; there is no broad O–H absorption ($3200$–$3550\ \text{cm}^{-1}$ or $2500$–$3000\ \text{cm}^{-1}$), so it is not an alcohol or carboxylic acid.
- **$^1$H NMR:** only one signal (at about 2.1 ppm, typical of H on C next to C=O), so all six H atoms are in one environment — the molecule is symmetrical. This rules out propanal (three environments, including an aldehyde H near 9–10 ppm).

questions.question: An unknown organic compound has been identified as propanone, $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3$. Draw and name an isomer of this compound.
questions.answer:
**Propanal**, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CHO}$ — a functional group isomer (an aldehyde, molecular formula $\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\text{O}$). Structural formula: $\text{CH}_3$–$\text{CH}_2$–C(=O)–H, with the C=O at the end of the chain bonded to one H.

(Other correct isomers include prop-2-en-1-ol, $\text{CH}_2\text{=CHCH}_2\text{OH}$.)

questions.question:
The following data shows the boiling points of primary alcohols and alkanes.

| Alkane | Boiling point (°C) | Alcohol | Boiling point (°C) |
|---|---|---|---|
| methane | −164 | methanol | 65 |
| ethane | −89 | ethanol | 79 |
| propane | −42 | 1-propanol | 97 |
| butane | −1 | 1-butanol | 117 |
| pentane | 36 | 1-pentanol | 138 |
| octane | 125 | 1-octanol | 195 |

Graph the data and explain the trends in this data.
questions.answer:
**Graph:** boiling point (°C, from −200 to 250) against number of carbon atoms (1 to 8), with the points for each series joined by a line (or smooth curve) and each line labelled (see graph). The x-axis must leave space for 6 and 7 carbons.

**Trend 1 — boiling point increases with chain length in both series.** As the number of carbon atoms increases, molecules have more electrons and a larger surface area, so the dispersion forces between molecules are stronger. More energy is needed to separate the molecules, so the boiling point increases.

**Trend 2 — each alcohol has a much higher boiling point than the alkane with the same number of carbons.** Alkanes are non-polar and have only dispersion forces. Alcohols have a polar –OH group, so in addition to dispersion forces their molecules form hydrogen bonds with each other, which are much stronger. More energy is needed to overcome these, so alcohols boil at higher temperatures.

**Trend 3 — the difference between the two series decreases as chain length increases** (e.g. 229 °C for C1 but 70 °C for C8). As the hydrocarbon chain grows, dispersion forces make up a larger share of the total intermolecular forces, so the single –OH group (hydrogen bonding) has a relatively smaller effect.

questions.question:
Sulfur trioxide, $\text{SO}_3$, is made by the reaction of sulfur dioxide, $\text{SO}_2$, and oxygen, $\text{O}_2$, in the presence of a catalyst, according to the equation below.

$$2\text{SO}_2(g) + \text{O}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{SO}_3(g) \qquad \Delta H < 0$$

In a closed system in the presence of the catalyst, the reaction achieves equilibrium at 1000 K. A mixture of 2.00 mol of $\text{SO}_2(g)$ and 2.00 mol of $\text{O}_2(g)$ was placed in a 4.00 L evacuated, sealed vessel and kept at 1000 K until equilibrium was reached. At equilibrium, the vessel was found to contain 1.66 mol of $\text{SO}_3(g)$.

Calculate the equilibrium constant, $K_{eq}$, at 1000 K.

A student is given 1 L of a 0.01 mol/L solution of calcium chloride. Solid KOH is added (assume that the addition of KOH does not change the volume of the solution). $K_{sp}(\text{Ca(OH)}_2) = 5.02 \times 10^{-6}$ at $25^\circ\text{C}$.

How many grams of solid KOH will have to be added before a precipitate is formed?
questions.answer:
$$\text{Ca(OH)}_2(s) \rightleftharpoons \text{Ca}^{2+}(aq) + 2\text{OH}^-(aq) \qquad K_{sp} = [\text{Ca}^{2+}][\text{OH}^-]^2$$

A precipitate just forms when the ionic product reaches $K_{sp}$. With $[\text{Ca}^{2+}] = 0.01$ mol/L:

$$[\text{OH}^-] = \sqrt{\frac{5.02 \times 10^{-6}}{0.01}} = 0.0224\ \text{mol/L}$$

In 1 L, $n(\text{KOH}) = 0.0224$ mol. $M(\text{KOH}) = 39.10 + 16.00 + 1.008 = 56.108$ g/mol.

$m = 0.0224 \times 56.108 = 1.26$ g

questions.question:
A student is given 1 L of a 0.01 mol/L solution of calcium chloride. Solid KOH is added (assume that the addition of KOH does not change the volume of the solution). $K_{sp}(\text{Ca(OH)}_2) = 5.02 \times 10^{-6}$ at $25^\circ\text{C}$.

Precipitation of $\text{Ca(OH)}_2$ just begins when $[\text{OH}^-] = 0.0224$ mol/L. What will be the pH of the solution immediately before the precipitate starts to form?

A student wanted to calculate the heat of combustion of butane. They used a spirit burner containing butane to heat up a 120 g container of water and the following graph of temperature change was obtained.

At the start of the experiment the mass of the spirit burner was 373.156 g and it was 372.643 g at the end of the experiment.

The theoretical molar heat of combustion for butane is $\Delta H_{comb} = -2877$ kJ/mol. (Specific heat capacity of water $= 4.18 \times 10^{3}\ \text{J kg}^{-1}\ \text{K}^{-1}$.)

Explain, using quantitative data from your calculations, the reasons for the percentage difference between the experimental and theoretical values and suggest ways that this difference could be minimised.
questions.answer:
**Calculation**

$\Delta T = 50.0 - 20.0 = 30.0$ °C (from when heating started to when heating was completed)

$q = mc\Delta T = 0.120 \times 4.18 \times 10^{3} \times 30.0 = 1.505 \times 10^{4}$ J $= 15.05$ kJ

Mass of butane burnt $= 373.156 - 372.643 = 0.513$ g; $n(\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}) = \dfrac{0.513}{58.12} = 8.83 \times 10^{-3}$ mol

$\Delta H_{comb} = -\dfrac{15.05}{8.83 \times 10^{-3}} = -1.70 \times 10^{3}$ kJ/mol (about $-1705$ kJ/mol)

Percentage difference $= \dfrac{2877 - 1705}{2877} \times 100 = 40.7\%$ — the experimental value is about 41% lower in magnitude.

**Reasons**

- **Heat loss to the surroundings:** much of the heat released by the flame heats the surrounding air, the container and the burner, rather than the water. Only the heat absorbed by the water is counted in $q$, so $q$ — and hence $\Delta H$ — is too small. The graph also shows the water losing heat to the surroundings (cooling from 50 °C to 40 °C after heating stopped), so heat was also being lost during heating.
- **Incomplete combustion:** with a limited oxygen supply some butane forms CO and soot (C) instead of $\text{CO}_2$, releasing less energy per mole than the theoretical (complete combustion) value.
- **Mass loss not due to combustion:** some fuel may evaporate from the burner without burning, so the moles "burnt" is overestimated, making $\Delta H$ smaller.

**Improvements**

- Shield the apparatus from draughts (e.g. a draught shield around the burner and can), put a lid on the container, and keep the flame close to the base of the container, so more heat goes into the water.
- Use a metal (e.g. copper) container and include its heat capacity in the calculation.
- Ensure a good oxygen supply (adjust the flame/wick so it burns blue, not yellow) to reduce incomplete combustion.
- Cap the burner when not burning and weigh it immediately to minimise evaporation losses; repeat the experiment and average the results.

questions.question:
Rain with a pH of less than 4.4 is classified as acid rain. Acid rain forms when acidic oxides such as $\text{SO}_2$ dissolve in rainwater to form sulfuric acid.

A 100.0 mL sample of rainwater was collected and diluted to 250 mL with distilled water. 25.0 mL aliquots of diluted rainwater were used in the titration with standardised sodium hydroxide solution.

The sodium hydroxide was standardised against a $3.76 \times 10^{-5}$ mol/L HCl solution. An average titre of 21.3 mL of this acid was required to neutralise 25.0 mL aliquots of NaOH solution.
