$$\text{Pb}^{2+}(aq) + 2\text{SCN}^-(aq) \rightleftharpoons \text{Pb(SCN)}_2(s)$$
**Moles before and after precipitation:**

| Quantity | Calculation | Moles |
|---|---|---|
| $\text{Pb(SCN)}_2$ precipitated | $\dfrac{2.19}{323.38}$ | $6.772 \times 10^{-3}$ |
| KSCN added | $\dfrac{2.53}{97.19}$ | $2.603 \times 10^{-2}$ |
| $\text{Pb}^{2+}$ added | $0.108 \times 0.125$ | $1.350 \times 10^{-2}$ |
| $\text{Pb}^{2+}$ left in solution | $0.01350 - 0.006772$ | $6.728 \times 10^{-3}$ |
| $\text{SCN}^-$ left in solution | $0.02603 - 2(0.006772)$ | $1.249 \times 10^{-2}$ |

**Concentrations** (total volume $= 0.2500 + 0.125 = 0.375$ L):
- $[\text{Pb}^{2+}] = \dfrac{6.728 \times 10^{-3}}{0.375} = 1.794 \times 10^{-2}$ mol L$^{-1}$
- $[\text{SCN}^-] = \dfrac{1.249 \times 10^{-2}}{0.375} = 3.330 \times 10^{-2}$ mol L$^{-1}$

**$K_{sp}$:**
$$K_{sp} = [\text{Pb}^{2+}][\text{SCN}^-]^2 = (1.794 \times 10^{-2})(3.330 \times 10^{-2})^2 = 1.99 \times 10^{-5}$$

questions.question: The reaction pathway shown begins with hex-3-ene. Hex-3-ene reacts with HBr(aq) to give compound J, and is converted to hexan-3-ol. Hexan-3-ol reacts with acidified permanganate ($\text{H}^+/\text{MnO}_4^-$) to give compound K, and with compound M in the presence of $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4(l)$ to give compound L (structure shown). Justify the identification of compounds J, M and K.
questions.answer:
**J is 3-bromohexane**, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CHBrCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$. HBr adds across the C=C double bond of hex-3-ene (an addition reaction). The H bonds to one carbon of the double bond and the Br to the other. Hex-3-ene is symmetrical, so only one product forms.

**M is ethanoic acid**, $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$. Compound L is the ester hexan-3-yl ethanoate, $\text{CH}_3\text{COOCH(CH}_2\text{CH}_3)\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$. An ester forms when an alcohol reacts with a carboxylic acid, with concentrated sulfuric acid as a catalyst (esterification). The alkyl part of L comes from hexan-3-ol. The acid part, $\text{CH}_3\text{COO}-$, has two carbons, so the acid added must be ethanoic acid.

**K is hexan-3-one**, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$. Hexan-3-ol is a secondary alcohol, because its –OH carbon is bonded to two other carbons. Acidified permanganate oxidises secondary alcohols to ketones (the purple colour fades), and the ketone is not oxidised further.

questions.question: Draw an equation, using structural formulae, for the conversion of hex-3-ene to hexan-3-ol, indicating the reagent(s) required.
questions.answer:
Hydration of the alkene: water adds across the double bond, with dilute sulfuric acid (or phosphoric acid) as a catalyst and heat.
$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}{=}\text{CHCH}_2\text{CH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \xrightarrow{\text{dil. H}_2\text{SO}_4\ \text{catalyst}} \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH(OH)CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$$
(All C–H bonds are drawn out in the full structural formulae.)

questions.question:
A student performs an experiment to determine the concentration of a solution of hypochlorous acid, HOCl ($K_a = 3.5 \times 10^{-8}$). The student starts with 25.00 mL of the acid in a conical flask and titrates it against a standardised solution of sodium hydroxide with a concentration of 1.47 mol L$^{-1}$. The equivalence point is reached after addition of 34.23 mL of NaOH.
$$\text{HOCl}(aq) + \text{OH}^-(aq) \rightarrow \text{OCl}^-(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$$

Calculate the concentration of the HOCl.
questions.answer:
At the equivalence point, $n(\text{HOCl}) = n(\text{NaOH})$ (1 : 1 ratio).

$n(\text{NaOH}) = 1.47 \times 0.03423 = 0.05032$ mol
$$c(\text{HOCl}) = \frac{0.05032}{0.02500} = 2.01\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$$

questions.question:
A student performs an experiment to determine the concentration of a solution of hypochlorous acid, HOCl ($K_a = 3.5 \times 10^{-8}$). The student starts with 25.00 mL of the acid in a conical flask and titrates it against a standardised solution of sodium hydroxide with a concentration of 1.47 mol L$^{-1}$. The equivalence point is reached after addition of 34.23 mL of NaOH.
$$\text{HOCl}(aq) + \text{OH}^-(aq) \rightarrow \text{OCl}^-(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$$

The concentration of the HOCl was found to be 2.01 mol L$^{-1}$. Determine the pH of the solution in the conical flask after the addition of 28.55 mL of NaOH.
questions.answer:
**Reaction (moles):**
- $n(\text{OH}^-) = 1.47 \times 0.02855 = 0.04197$ mol
- $n(\text{HOCl})_{\text{initial}} = 1.47 \times 0.03423 = 0.05032$ mol

| | HOCl | $\text{OH}^-$ | $\text{OCl}^-$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| Initial | 0.05032 | 0.04197 | 0 |
| Change | $-0.04197$ | $-0.04197$ | $+0.04197$ |
| End | 0.00835 | 0 | 0.04197 |

**Concentrations** (total volume $= 25.00 + 28.55 = 53.55$ mL):
- $[\text{HOCl}] = \dfrac{0.00835}{0.05355} = 0.1559$ mol L$^{-1}$
- $[\text{OCl}^-] = \dfrac{0.04197}{0.05355} = 0.7837$ mol L$^{-1}$

**Equilibrium:** $\text{HOCl} \rightleftharpoons \text{H}^+ + \text{OCl}^-$. Because $K_a$ is very small, the change $x$ is negligible:
$$K_a = \frac{[\text{H}^+][\text{OCl}^-]}{[\text{HOCl}]} \Rightarrow 3.5 \times 10^{-8} = \frac{x(0.7837)}{0.1559}$$
$$[\text{H}^+] = x = 6.96 \times 10^{-9}\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$$
$$\text{pH} = -\log_{10}(6.96 \times 10^{-9}) = 8.16$$

(Equivalently, for this buffer: $\text{pH} = \text{p}K_a + \log_{10}\dfrac{[\text{OCl}^-]}{[\text{HOCl}]} = 7.46 + 0.70 = 8.16$.)

questions.question:
A student performs an experiment to determine the concentration of a solution of hypochlorous acid, HOCl ($K_a = 3.5 \times 10^{-8}$). The student starts with 25.00 mL of the acid in a conical flask and titrates it against a standardised solution of sodium hydroxide with a concentration of 1.47 mol L$^{-1}$. The equivalence point is reached after addition of 34.23 mL of NaOH.
$$\text{HOCl}(aq) + \text{OH}^-(aq) \rightarrow \text{OCl}^-(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$$

From these results the student calculated the concentration of HOCl to be 2.01 mol L$^{-1}$. The actual concentration of the HOCl is found to be 1.85 mol L$^{-1}$. Qualitatively discuss whether the following error may have contributed to the student's results: *The student rinsed the burette with distilled water instead of NaOH solution before filling it with NaOH.*
questions.answer:
Rinsing with distilled water leaves water in the burette, which dilutes the NaOH to below 1.47 mol L$^{-1}$. More of the diluted NaOH is needed to reach the equivalence point, so the titre (34.23 mL) is larger than it should be. In the calculation the student still uses 1.47 mol L$^{-1}$ multiplied by this larger volume. That overestimates the moles of NaOH, and so the moles and concentration of HOCl.

So this error makes the calculated concentration too high, and it could have contributed to the student's result: 2.01 mol L$^{-1}$ is higher than the actual 1.85 mol L$^{-1}$.

To check the size: the actual $n(\text{HOCl}) = 1.85 \times 0.02500 = 0.0463$ mol, which needs only 31.5 mL of 1.47 mol L$^{-1}$ NaOH. A 34.23 mL titre means the NaOH was really about 1.35 mol L$^{-1}$, roughly 8% diluted. Leftover rinse water could plausibly cause that.

*Note: the paper's marking guideline was written for a version with an actual concentration of 2.25 mol L$^{-1}$ and concludes that the error could not explain the result. With the value 1.85 mol L$^{-1}$ printed in the exam, the conclusion is reversed.*

questions.question:
A halogenated organic compound M with a molar mass of 94.54 g mol$^{-1}$ is known to produce TWO products, compounds N and O, when heated with concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$:
$$\text{M} \xrightarrow{\text{conc. H}_2\text{SO}_4} \text{N} + \text{O}$$
A chemist obtained the infrared and mass spectra for compound M (first image), and the proton and carbon-13 NMR spectra for products N and O (second image). Proton NMR data are given in the table (third image).

Draw the structure and name each of the compounds M, N and O. Justify your answer with reference to all the information provided.
questions.answer:
**Compound M: 1-chloropropan-2-ol**, $\text{ClCH}_2\text{–CH(OH)–CH}_3$

- **IR:** the very broad, strong absorption centred near 3400 cm$^{-1}$ is an O–H stretch, which shows an alcohol. There is no strong C=O absorption near 1700 cm$^{-1}$.
- **Molecular ion:** the mass spectrum has a small molecular ion peak at $m/z = 94$ and a peak at 96 in about a 3 : 1 ratio. This is the pattern of the $^{35}\text{Cl}$/$^{37}\text{Cl}$ isotopes, so M has one Cl atom. $\text{C}_3\text{H}_7\text{ClO}$ has $M = 3(12.01) + 7(1.008) + 35.45 + 16.00 = 94.54$ g mol$^{-1}$, which matches.
- **Fragments:**

| $m/z$ | Fragment | Information |
|---|---|---|
| 79/81 | $[\text{M} - \text{CH}_3]^+$ | contains Cl |
| 49/51 (base peak) | $[\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}]^+$ | Cl is on a terminal $\text{CH}_2$ |
| 45 | $[\text{CH}_3\text{CHOH}]^+$ | no Cl; OH on the middle carbon next to the $\text{CH}_3$ |
| 15 | $[\text{CH}_3]^+$ | methyl group |

- **Reaction:** concentrated sulfuric acid dehydrates alcohols. Removing the –OH from C2 with an H from either neighbouring carbon gives two different alkenes, $\text{C}_3\text{H}_5\text{Cl}$. This explains why there are two products.

**Compound N: 1-chloroprop-1-ene**, $\text{ClCH{=}CH–CH}_3$ (H removed from the $\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$ carbon)

- **$^{13}$C NMR:** 3 signals. The signals at about 130 and 105 ppm are the two sp$^2$ carbons of a C=C. The signal at about 15 ppm is an alkyl $\text{CH}_3$ that is not attached to Cl.
- **$^1$H NMR:**

| Shift (ppm) | Integration | Splitting | Assignment |
|---|---|---|---|
| ~1.8 | 3H | doublet | $\text{CH}_3$ next to one H |
| ~5.7 | 1H | doublet | alkene =CHCl, next to one H |
| ~6.0 | 1H | multiplet | alkene =CH–, coupled to both the =CHCl and the $\text{CH}_3$ |

This gives the chain Cl–CH=CH–CH$_3$.

**Compound O: 3-chloroprop-1-ene**, $\text{CH}_2{=}\text{CH–CH}_2\text{Cl}$ (H removed from the $\text{CH}_3$ carbon)

- **$^{13}$C NMR:** 3 signals. The signals at about 135 and 118 ppm are the C=C carbons. The signal at about 45 ppm is an sp$^3$ carbon shifted downfield by the electronegative Cl, which shows a $\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$ group.
- **$^1$H NMR:**

| Shift (ppm) | Integration | Splitting | Assignment |
|---|---|---|---|
| ~4.0 | 2H | doublet | $\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$ next to one H |
| ~5.0 | 2H | doublet | =$\text{CH}_2$ |
| ~6.2 | 1H | multiplet | =CH–, between the two $\text{CH}_2$ groups |

This gives the chain $\text{CH}_2$=CH–$\text{CH}_2$Cl.

questions.question:
A commercial disinfectant is reported to have two active ingredients, hydrogen peroxide ($\text{H}_2\text{O}_2$) and peracetic acid ($\text{CH}_3\text{COOOH}$), at concentrations of 4% and 12% (w/v) respectively. A titration experiment was carried out to confirm the accuracy of these values.

A 10.00 mL sample of the disinfectant solution was transferred to a 100 mL volumetric flask, which was filled to the mark with demineralised water. 20.00 mL of the resultant solution was transferred to a conical flask containing 5.000 mL of 3.000 mol L$^{-1}$ sulfuric acid and titrated with a 0.2491 mol L$^{-1}$ cerium sulfate solution.

Equation 1: $\text{H}_2\text{O}_2(aq) + 2\text{Ce(SO}_4)_2(aq) \rightarrow \text{Ce}_2(\text{SO}_4)_3(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4(aq) + \text{O}_2(g)$

| Titre | Volume of $\text{Ce(SO}_4)_2$ added (mL) |
|---|---|
| 1 | 21.65 |
| 2 | 21.15 |
| 3 | 21.20 |
| 4 | 21.30 |

Immediately after, 5.000 mL of a 20% (w/v) potassium iodide solution was added to the conical flask containing titre 4. This reacts with the sulfuric acid to produce hydroiodic acid, which then reduces the peracetic acid present in the sample and forms iodine.

Equation 2: $2\text{KI}(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4(aq) \rightarrow 2\text{HI}(aq) + \text{K}_2\text{SO}_4(aq)$

Equation 3: $\text{CH}_3\text{COOOH}(aq) + 2\text{HI}(aq) \rightarrow \text{I}_2(aq) + \text{CH}_3\text{COOH}(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$

The resultant iodine solution was titrated with a 0.2250 mol L$^{-1}$ solution of sodium thiosulfate, and a titre volume of 27.35 mL was required to reach the end point.

Equation 4: $\text{I}_2(aq) + 2\text{Na}_2\text{S}_2\text{O}_3(aq) \rightarrow \text{Na}_2\text{S}_4\text{O}_6(aq) + 2\text{NaI}(aq)$

Do the results of this experiment support the reported concentration values? Support your answer with calculations.
questions.answer:
**Hydrogen peroxide**

Titre 1 is an outlier (rough titre), so average titres 2–4:
$$V_{\text{avg}} = \frac{21.15 + 21.20 + 21.30}{3} = 21.22\ \text{mL}$$

$n(\text{Ce}^{4+}) = 0.2491 \times 0.02122 = 5.286 \times 10^{-3}$ mol

$n(\text{H}_2\text{O}_2) = \tfrac12 \times 5.286 \times 10^{-3} = 2.643 \times 10^{-3}$ mol in 20.00 mL of diluted solution

Scale up through the dilution:
- In 100 mL of diluted solution (= 10.00 mL of disinfectant): $2.643 \times 10^{-3} \times 5 = 1.321 \times 10^{-2}$ mol
- In 100 mL of original disinfectant: $1.321 \times 10^{-2} \times 10 = 0.1321$ mol

$m(\text{H}_2\text{O}_2) = 0.1321 \times 34.016 = 4.49$ g per 100 mL, i.e. **4.5% (w/v)**

**Peracetic acid**

$n(\text{S}_2\text{O}_3^{2-}) = 0.2250 \times 0.02735 = 6.154 \times 10^{-3}$ mol

$n(\text{I}_2) = \tfrac12 \times 6.154 \times 10^{-3} = 3.077 \times 10^{-3}$ mol, so $n(\text{CH}_3\text{COOOH}) = 3.077 \times 10^{-3}$ mol in 20.00 mL

In 100 mL of original disinfectant: $3.077 \times 10^{-3} \times 5 \times 10 = 0.1538$ mol

$m(\text{CH}_3\text{COOOH}) = 0.1538 \times 76.05 = 11.70$ g per 100 mL, i.e. **11.7% (w/v)**

**Evaluation**

The measured peracetic acid concentration (11.7%) is within about 2.5% of the reported 12%, so the results support the stated peracetic acid content. The measured hydrogen peroxide concentration (4.5%) is about 12% higher than the reported 4%. So the results do not closely support the stated hydrogen peroxide value; the disinfectant contains somewhat more $\text{H}_2\text{O}_2$ than reported.

*Note: the paper's sample answer gets the same values (4.494% and 11.70%) but concludes the opposite, that the $\text{H}_2\text{O}_2$ value is accurate and the peracetic acid value is not. The percentage differences show the reverse is true.*

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an appropriate safety precaution for an experiment investigating the reaction of cyclohexene with bromine water in a school laboratory?
options: Conduct reaction in a fume cupboard.
Collect reaction products in a waste bottle.
questions.answer: Goggles and apron protect against splashes of bromine water, the fume cupboard removes toxic bromine and cyclohexene vapours, and organic/halogenated products must be collected in a waste bottle (not poured down the sink). Using large beakers is not a safety precaution — small quantities in test tubes should be used.

questions.question:
Which of the following rows correctly identifies the changes in entropy and enthalpy for combustion and photosynthesis?

| | Entropy change: combustion | Entropy change: photosynthesis | Enthalpy change: combustion | Enthalpy change: photosynthesis |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A. | Increases | Decreases | Endothermic | Exothermic |
| B. | Decreases | Increases | Exothermic | Endothermic |
| C. | Increases | Decreases | Exothermic | Endothermic |
| D. | Decreases | Increases | Endothermic | Exothermic |
questions.answer: Combustion converts a large ordered fuel molecule into many small gas molecules (entropy increases) and releases energy (exothermic). Photosynthesis is the reverse: small molecules ($\text{CO}_2$, $\text{H}_2\text{O}$) form one ordered glucose molecule (entropy decreases), and it absorbs light energy (endothermic).

questions.question:
Which of the following correctly matches the molecular shape around the carbon atom in each bond?

| | C–C | C=C | C≡C |
|---|---|---|---|
| A. | Linear | Trigonal planar | Tetrahedral |
| B. | Tetrahedral | Trigonal planar | Linear |
| C. | Tetrahedral | Trigonal planar | Bent |
| D. | Bent | Linear | Trigonal planar |
questions.answer: A carbon with only single bonds has 4 bonding regions (tetrahedral); a carbon in a C=C double bond has 3 regions (trigonal planar); a carbon in a C≡C triple bond has 2 regions (linear).

questions.question: Which of the following titration curves shows the addition of a strong base to a weak acid?
questions.answer: Adding base makes the pH rise, so the curve must increase (A or C). A weak acid starts at a moderately low pH (about 3–5, not 1) with a buffer region, and its equivalence point is above 7 because the conjugate base is basic. This is curve C (A starts at pH 1 — a strong acid).

questions.question:
The table below shows three separate tests used to identify a dilute, aqueous sample of a compound.

| Test number | Test | Observation |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Add $\text{HNO}_3$ to the sample | No bubbles |
| 2 | Flame test | Apple green |
| 3 | Add $\text{Cl}^-$ | No precipitate forms |

Which compound would produce the observations shown?
questions.answer: An apple-green flame identifies $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ (copper gives blue-green). No bubbles with acid rules out a carbonate (which would release $\text{CO}_2$), and $\text{BaCl}_2$ is soluble so no precipitate forms with $\text{Cl}^-$. The compound is barium nitrate.

questions.question:
Hydrogen sulfide can be removed from natural gas according to the equation below.

$$2\text{H}_2\text{S}(g) + \text{SO}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 3\text{S}(s) + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(g) \qquad \Delta H = -145\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$

Which of the following would maximise the removal of hydrogen sulfide from this system?
options: Decreasing the volume of the vessel
Removing some sulfur from the system
Adding water vapour to the system
questions.answer: There are 3 mol of gas on the left and 2 mol of gas on the right (sulfur is a solid). Decreasing the volume increases the pressure, so the equilibrium shifts right (fewer gas moles), removing more $\text{H}_2\text{S}$. Removing solid sulfur has no effect; increasing temperature favours the endothermic reverse reaction; adding water vapour shifts the equilibrium left.

questions.question:
Methyl methacrylate is a monomer that is able to undergo polymerisation. Its structural formula is shown.

What type of polymerisation is most likely to occur for methyl methacrylate?
questions.answer: The monomer contains a C=C double bond and has no pair of functional groups (e.g. –OH and –COOH) that could eliminate a small molecule, so it undergoes addition polymerisation (forming poly(methyl methacrylate), Perspex).

questions.question: A solution was known to contain either potassium phosphate or sodium iodide. Which of the following could be used to identify the salt present in the given solution?
questions.answer:
Adding lead(II) nitrate gives a precipitate with both anions, but of different colours: lead(II) phosphate is white while lead(II) iodide is bright yellow, so the salt can be identified. Iron(II) carbonate and magnesium hydroxide are insoluble, so they cannot supply ions to test with.

(The school's marking guidelines also accepted C: by the solubility rules, copper(II) acetate precipitates only the phosphate.)

questions.question:
At a particular temperature, iodine trichloride dissociates into iodine gas and chlorine gas according to the equation below.

$$2\text{ICl}_3(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{I}_2(g) + 3\text{Cl}_2(g) \qquad \Delta H = 240\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$

Initially, 0.60 mol of iodine trichloride was introduced into a 500 mL container and allowed to reach equilibrium. The concentration of chlorine gas at equilibrium was 0.60 mol L$^{-1}$.

What is the value of $K_{eq}$ at this temperature?

A manufacturer carried out tests to find the yield of an equilibrium reaction at different temperatures and pressures. The graph shows the yield of C (%) against temperature (°C) at pressures of 25, 60 and 150 atmospheres.

Which of the following equations best matches the results shown in the graph?
questions.answer: The yield of C increases with temperature, so the forward reaction is endothermic ($\Delta H > 0$). The yield is highest at the lowest pressure, so the forward reaction produces more moles of gas (2 mol → 3 mol). Hence D.

questions.question: Ascorbic acid (vitamin C), a monoprotic acid, has the molecular formula $\text{C}_6\text{H}_8\text{O}_6$ and a $K_a$ value of $8 \times 10^{-5}$ at 25°C. A tablet containing 250 mg of vitamin C was dissolved in 100 mL of water at 25°C. What is the pH of this solution?
questions.answer:
$M(\text{C}_6\text{H}_8\text{O}_6) = 176.12$ g mol$^{-1}$, so $n = 0.250/176.12 = 1.419 \times 10^{-3}$ mol and $c = 1.419 \times 10^{-2}$ mol L$^{-1}$.

Assuming little dissociation, $[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+] = \sqrt{K_a c} = \sqrt{8 \times 10^{-5} \times 1.419 \times 10^{-2}} = 1.07 \times 10^{-3}$ mol L$^{-1}$, so $\text{pH} = -\log_{10}(1.07 \times 10^{-3}) = 2.97$.

questions.question: The complete combustion of propanol releases more heat per mole of fuel compared to the complete combustion of methanol. Which of the following statements best explains this phenomenon?
options: More energy is required to break the bonds in the propanol molecules.
More molecules of carbon dioxide are formed in the combustion of propanol.
More molecules of oxygen are required in the combustion of propanol.
The boiling point for propanol is higher.
questions.answer: Heat is released when bonds form. Each mole of propanol forms 3 mol of $\text{CO}_2$ (and 4 mol of $\text{H}_2\text{O}$) compared with 1 mol of $\text{CO}_2$ for methanol, so many more strong C=O (and O–H) bonds are formed, releasing more energy per mole of fuel. (Option A would make it release *less* heat.)

questions.question: The enthalpy of combustion for ethyne is $-1301$ kJ mol$^{-1}$. What is the mass of ethyne required to produce 20 MJ of heat energy when combusted?

The following equilibrium lies to the product side:

$$\text{HSO}_4^-(aq) + \text{HCO}_3^-(aq) \rightleftharpoons \text{SO}_4^{2-}(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{CO}_3(aq)$$

Which of the following species is the conjugate acid?
questions.answer: $\text{HCO}_3^-$ accepts a proton from $\text{HSO}_4^-$ (it is the base), forming its conjugate acid $\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3$.

questions.question:
The following equilibrium lies to the product side:

$$\text{HSO}_4^-(aq) + \text{HCO}_3^-(aq) \rightleftharpoons \text{SO}_4^{2-}(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{CO}_3(aq)$$

Which of the following species would have the highest $K_a$?
questions.answer: The two acids in the equilibrium are $\text{HSO}_4^-$ (forward) and $\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3$ (reverse). Since the equilibrium lies to the product side, $\text{HSO}_4^-$ donates protons more readily than $\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3$, so $\text{HSO}_4^-$ is the stronger acid with the highest $K_a$.

questions.question: What is the IUPAC name of the compound shown (skeletal formula)?
questions.answer: The longest chain containing the C=C has 7 carbons (from the end of the double-bond branch through to the ethyl end). Numbering from the end nearest the double bond: the double bond starts at C2, a propyl group is on C4 and a methyl group on C5 → 5-methyl-4-propylhept-2-ene.

questions.question:
The table below shows the conductivity of a range of 0.01 mol L$^{-1}$ solutions.

| Solution | Conductivity (S m$^2$) |
|---|---|
| HBr | 411 |
| KOH | 257 |
| HCOOH | 43 |
| $\text{NH}_3$ | 11 |
| $\text{H}_3\text{BO}_3$ | 0.14 |

Using the table, which of the following statements is correct?
options: KOH is a stronger acid than HCOOH.
$\text{H}_3\text{BO}_3$ has low conductivity because it is triprotic.
HBr has a high degree of ionisation.
The $\text{OH}^-$ ions are better conductors than $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ ions.
questions.answer: At equal concentration, conductivity depends on the concentration of ions. HBr has the highest conductivity because it is a strong acid that ionises completely. KOH is a base, not an acid; $\text{H}_3\text{BO}_3$ conducts poorly because it is a very weak acid (not because it is triprotic); and HBr (giving $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$) conducts better than KOH (giving $\text{OH}^-$), so D is false.

questions.question: Which of the following compounds has the lowest molar solubility in water? (Use $K_{sp}$ values from the data sheet.)
questions.answer:
Barium nitrate is soluble. For the others, find the molar solubility $s$ from $K_{sp}$:

- $\text{Ca(OH)}_2$: $K_{sp} = 4s^3 = 5.02 \times 10^{-6} \Rightarrow s = 1.1 \times 10^{-2}$ mol L$^{-1}$
- $\text{FePO}_4$: $K_{sp} = s^2 = 9.91 \times 10^{-16} \Rightarrow s = 3.1 \times 10^{-8}$ mol L$^{-1}$
- $\text{Mg}_3(\text{PO}_4)_2$: $K_{sp} = 108 s^5 = 1.04 \times 10^{-24} \Rightarrow s = 6.3 \times 10^{-6}$ mol L$^{-1}$

Although magnesium phosphate has the smallest $K_{sp}$, iron(III) phosphate has the lowest molar solubility.

questions.question:
The esters of glycerol (propane-1,2,3-triol), which can be referred to as fats or oils, can be used to make soaps. This is done by reacting the ester functional groups with hydroxide ions to form glycerol and the carboxylate ions. The diagram shows the structural formula of a particular fat used to make soap (glycerol esterified with three $\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_{14}\text{COOH}$ chains, $\text{C}_{51}\text{H}_{98}\text{O}_6$).

A student dissolved 8.0 g of sodium hydroxide in 50 mL of water and then added 10 g of the fat. After the reaction mixture was heated, the soap product was extracted and found to weigh 6.45 g. The percentage yield in this process is closest to
questions.answer:
$$\text{C}_{51}\text{H}_{98}\text{O}_6 + 3\text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{C}_3\text{H}_5(\text{OH})_3 + 3\text{NaC}_{16}\text{H}_{31}\text{O}_2$$

$n(\text{NaOH}) = 8.0/40.00 = 0.200$ mol (excess). $n(\text{fat}) = 10/807.29 = 0.01239$ mol, so theoretical $n(\text{soap}) = 3 \times 0.01239 = 0.03716$ mol.

Actual $n(\text{soap}) = 6.45/278.40 = 0.02317$ mol, so yield $= 0.02317/0.03716 \times 100 = 62\%$.

questions.question: For polyvinyl chloride (PVC) and polytetrafluoroethene (PTFE), draw the structural formula of the monomer and of the polymer, and give one property and one use of each polymer.
questions.answer:
| | Polyvinyl chloride | Polytetrafluoroethene |
|---|---|---|
| Monomer | chloroethene, $\text{CH}_2{=}\text{CHCl}$ | tetrafluoroethene, $\text{CF}_2{=}\text{CF}_2$ |
| Polymer | $-[\text{CH}_2-\text{CHCl}]_n-$ | $-[\text{CF}_2-\text{CF}_2]_n-$ |
| Property | e.g. strong, rigid (flexible when plasticised), water-resistant | e.g. non-stick (very low friction), chemically inert, high melting point, waterproof |
| Use | e.g. water pipes, electrical wire insulation, raincoats, floor tiles | e.g. non-stick frying pan coatings, waterproof fabric |

The structural formulae are shown in the diagram.

questions.question: A student mixed 500.0 mL of a 0.00123 mol L$^{-1}$ solution of $\text{FeF}_2$ with 500.0 mL of a 0.00314 mol L$^{-1}$ solution of KOH at 25°C. Using calculations, determine if a precipitate will be formed from the mixture. ($K_{sp}(\text{Fe(OH)}_2) = 4.87 \times 10^{-17}$)
questions.answer:
$n(\text{Fe}^{2+}) = 0.00123 \times 0.5000 = 6.15 \times 10^{-4}$ mol; $n(\text{OH}^-) = 0.00314 \times 0.5000 = 1.57 \times 10^{-3}$ mol.

The total volume is 1.000 L, so $[\text{Fe}^{2+}] = 6.15 \times 10^{-4}$ mol L$^{-1}$ and $[\text{OH}^-] = 1.57 \times 10^{-3}$ mol L$^{-1}$.

$$\text{Fe(OH)}_2(s) \rightleftharpoons \text{Fe}^{2+}(aq) + 2\text{OH}^-(aq) \qquad K_{sp} = [\text{Fe}^{2+}][\text{OH}^-]^2$$

$$Q = (6.15 \times 10^{-4})(1.57 \times 10^{-3})^2 = 1.52 \times 10^{-9}$$

Since $Q = 1.52 \times 10^{-9} > K_{sp} = 4.87 \times 10^{-17}$, a precipitate of iron(II) hydroxide will form.

questions.question: Outline ONE advantage and ONE disadvantage of biofuels when compared to fossil fuel alternatives.
questions.answer:
**Advantage:** biofuels are made from renewable resources such as plant material (e.g. sugar cane, corn) that can be regrown, whereas fossil fuels are finite. (Also accepted: they burn more cleanly — less incomplete combustion, so less CO and soot; they are more biodegradable if spilled.) Note that the net release of $\text{CO}_2$ is lower only because $\text{CO}_2$ is absorbed while the crops grow — combustion itself still produces $\text{CO}_2$.

**Disadvantage:** biofuels such as ethanol release less energy per gram than petrol (lower heat of combustion), so more fuel is needed. (Also accepted: growing fuel crops uses farmland that could grow food, causing food shortages or land clearing; production by fermentation and distillation is slow and energy-intensive, making it expensive; some engines need modification.)

questions.question: Outline ONE economic and ONE environmental implication of obtaining and/or using hydrocarbons.
questions.answer:
**Economic:** the oil and gas industry employs millions of people worldwide, providing stable jobs and income, and contributes significant taxes and export revenue to the host country (it has also driven industrialisation and mass manufacturing).

**Environmental:** oil spills during extraction or transport can damage marine ecosystems and kill organisms; also, burning hydrocarbons releases $\text{CO}_2$ (contributing to the enhanced greenhouse effect) and pollutants such as CO, soot and $\text{NO}_x$ into the atmosphere.

questions.question:
Sodium hydroxide reacts with the weak acid oxalic acid according to the equation:

$$2\text{NaOH}(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{C}_2\text{O}_4(aq) \rightarrow \text{Na}_2\text{C}_2\text{O}_4(aq) + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$$

Explain why solutions of sodium oxalate are basic. Support your answer with a relevant chemical equation.
questions.answer:
In solution, sodium oxalate dissociates into $\text{Na}^+$ and $\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-}$ ions. The $\text{Na}^+$ ions are spectator ions and do not react with water, so they have no effect on pH. However, the oxalate ion is a weak base (the conjugate base of the weak acid $\text{HC}_2\text{O}_4^-$) and accepts a proton from water, producing hydroxide ions:

$$\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-}(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightleftharpoons \text{HC}_2\text{O}_4^-(aq) + \text{OH}^-(aq)$$

This increases $[\text{OH}^-]$ above $[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]$, so the solution is basic.

questions.question:
Sodium hydroxide reacts with the weak acid oxalic acid according to the equation:

$$2\text{NaOH}(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{C}_2\text{O}_4(aq) \rightarrow \text{Na}_2\text{C}_2\text{O}_4(aq) + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$$

A student wants to determine the concentration of a sample of oxalic acid using a standardised solution of sodium hydroxide. The student is provided with the following indicators.

| Indicator | Colour change | pH range over which colour changes |
|---|---|---|
| Bromocresol green | yellow–blue | 3.8 – 5.4 |
| 4-nitrophenol | colourless–yellow | 5.7 – 7.6 |
| Phenolphthalein | colourless–pink | 8.3 – 10.0 |

Using the table, determine the most appropriate indicator for this titration and justify your choice.
questions.answer:
Phenolphthalein.

This titration is between a strong base (NaOH) and a weak acid (oxalic acid), so the salt formed, sodium oxalate, is basic. Therefore the pH of the solution at the equivalence point is above 7, which falls within phenolphthalein's colour-change range of 8.3–10.0, so the end point will coincide with the equivalence point.

questions.question: Provide chemical equations to show the amphiprotic nature of the hydrogen oxalate ion, $\text{HC}_2\text{O}_4^-$.
questions.answer:
Acting as an acid (donating a proton):
$$\text{HC}_2\text{O}_4^-(aq) + \text{OH}^-(aq) \rightarrow \text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-}(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$$

Acting as a base (accepting a proton):
$$\text{HC}_2\text{O}_4^-(aq) + \text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq) \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{C}_2\text{O}_4(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$$

(Equations with water as the reacting species, e.g. $\text{HC}_2\text{O}_4^- + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-} + \text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ and $\text{HC}_2\text{O}_4^- + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{H}_2\text{C}_2\text{O}_4 + \text{OH}^-$, are also correct.)

questions.question: Benzoic acid, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOH}$, is used as a preservative in certain foods to prevent the growth of moulds. This acid has a $K_a$ value of $6.5 \times 10^{-5}$ at 25°C. How many grams of benzoic acid are needed to prepare 1.0 L of a solution with a pH of 2.80 at 25°C?
questions.answer:
$[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+] = 10^{-2.80} = 1.585 \times 10^{-3}$ mol L$^{-1}$ $= [\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COO}^-]$.

$$K_a = \frac{[\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COO}^-][\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]}{[\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOH}]} \Rightarrow [\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOH}]_{eq} = \frac{(1.585 \times 10^{-3})^2}{6.5 \times 10^{-5}} = 3.865 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$$

Initial concentration $= 3.865 \times 10^{-2} + 1.585 \times 10^{-3} = 4.023 \times 10^{-2}$ mol L$^{-1}$, so in 1.0 L, $n = 4.023 \times 10^{-2}$ mol.

$M(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOH}) = 7(12.01) + 6(1.008) + 2(16.00) = 122.12$ g mol$^{-1}$

$m = 4.023 \times 10^{-2} \times 122.12 = 4.91$ g

*(The school's solution adds the two concentrations as 0.04018 and gets 4.90 g; the correct sum is 0.04023, giving 4.91 g.)*

questions.question: Benzoic acid, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOH}$, is used as a preservative in certain foods to prevent the growth of moulds. This acid has a $K_a$ value of $6.5 \times 10^{-5}$ at 25°C. A solution of benzoic acid and sodium benzoate was made at 25°C and was measured to have a pH of 4.48. When NaOH was added to the solution, there was little change to the pH. This was also observed when HCl was added. Using a relevant chemical equation, explain these observations.
questions.answer:
The solution is a buffer: it contains significant amounts of both the weak acid and its conjugate base in equilibrium:

$$\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOH}(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightleftharpoons \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COO}^-(aq) + \text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq)$$

When NaOH is added, the $\text{OH}^-$ ions react with $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$, decreasing its concentration. By Le Chatelier's principle the equilibrium shifts to the right to counteract this, ionising more benzoic acid and replacing the $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$, so there is little change in pH.

When HCl is added, $[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]$ increases. The equilibrium shifts to the left, as benzoate ions react with the added $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ to form benzoic acid, consuming most of it, so again there is little change in pH. Because both the acid and its conjugate base are present in large amounts, the added $\text{OH}^-$ or $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ is consumed.

questions.question:
The pH of the oceans has been maintained by the following equilibria.

1. $\text{CO}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{CO}_2(aq)$
2. $\text{CO}_2(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightleftharpoons \text{H}_2\text{CO}_3(aq)$
3. $\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightleftharpoons \text{HCO}_3^-(aq) + \text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq)$

Since the start of the industrial age, the pH of the oceans has been decreasing. It is estimated that the pH of the ocean will fall from 8.14 to 7.90 over the next 50 years.

Using the equations provided, explain how the combustion of fossil fuels is responsible for the change in pH of the ocean.
questions.answer:
Combustion of fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide into the atmosphere, increasing $[\text{CO}_2(g)]$.

By Le Chatelier's principle, this increase causes equilibrium 1 to shift to the right (favouring the forward reaction), increasing $[\text{CO}_2(aq)]$. As a result, equilibrium 2 also shifts to the right, increasing $[\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3(aq)]$. Finally, equilibrium 3 shifts to the right to minimise this disturbance, increasing $[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]$.

Because $[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]$ increases, the pH of the ocean decreases ($\text{pH} = -\log_{10}[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]$).

questions.question:
The equilibrium between two different coloured Co(II) complex ions, $[\text{Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6]^{2+}$ and $[\text{CoCl}_4]^{2-}$, has been used by ecologists in qualitative tests to determine water content in soil. Solutions of cobalt chloride are pink, due to the formation of the complex ion $[\text{Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6]^{2+}$. The equilibrium is:

$$\underbrace{\text{CoCl}_4^{2-}(aq)}_{\text{blue}} + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightleftharpoons \underbrace{\text{Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6^{2+}(aq)}_{\text{pink}} + 4\text{Cl}^-(aq)$$

Using Le Chatelier's principle, explain the change in colour if drops of concentrated HCl were added to the system.
questions.answer: Adding concentrated HCl increases $[\text{Cl}^-]$. By Le Chatelier's principle, the system shifts to decrease $[\text{Cl}^-]$ by favouring the reverse reaction. As a result, $[\text{CoCl}_4^{2-}]$ increases (and $[\text{Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6^{2+}]$ decreases), so the solution becomes more blue (purple then blue).

questions.question:
The equilibrium between two different coloured Co(II) complex ions, $[\text{Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6]^{2+}$ and $[\text{CoCl}_4]^{2-}$, has been used by ecologists in qualitative tests to determine water content in soil. Solutions of cobalt chloride are pink, due to the formation of the complex ion $[\text{Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6]^{2+}$. The equilibrium is:

$$\underbrace{\text{CoCl}_4^{2-}(aq)}_{\text{blue}} + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightleftharpoons \underbrace{\text{Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6^{2+}(aq)}_{\text{pink}} + 4\text{Cl}^-(aq)$$

In a second experiment, a solution of cobalt chloride was prepared and separated into three test tubes. One test tube was placed in a beaker of water at room temperature, while the other two were placed in a beaker of ice water and a beaker of hot water, respectively. The following observations were made.

| | Ice water | Room temperature | Hot water |
|---|---|---|---|
| Colour of solution | pink | purple | blue |

Using your understanding of collision theory, explain the observations above.
questions.answer:
When the temperature increases, the kinetic energy of all particles increases, so collisions are more frequent and a greater proportion of collisions have energy greater than the activation energy — more successful collisions. Therefore the rates of **both** the forward and reverse reactions increase.

The proportional increase in rate is greater for the endothermic reaction, because it has the higher activation energy, so the endothermic reaction is favoured. Similarly, when the temperature decreases, the rates of both reactions decrease, but the endothermic reaction has a larger proportional decrease, so the exothermic reaction is favoured.

The solution is blue in hot water, so the reverse reaction (forming $\text{CoCl}_4^{2-}$) is favoured at high temperature — the reverse reaction is endothermic. In ice water the solution is pink, as the forward reaction (forming $\text{Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6^{2+}$), which is exothermic, is favoured. At room temperature, significant amounts of both the blue and pink ions are present, giving a purple colour.

questions.question: 150.0 mL of a 0.564 mol L$^{-1}$ barium hydroxide solution was placed in a well-insulated beaker. The temperature of the solution was 20.3°C. Subsequently, 400 mL of a 1.25 mol L$^{-1}$ nitric acid solution was placed in another beaker and brought to the same temperature. The two solutions were then mixed, and the final maximum temperature was recorded to be 23.7°C. Assume that the density of the solutions was 1.00 g mL$^{-1}$ (and the specific heat capacity $4.18 \times 10^{3}$ J kg$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$). Calculate the molar enthalpy of neutralisation.
questions.answer:
$q = mc\Delta T = (0.5500\ \text{kg})(4.18 \times 10^{3})(23.7 - 20.3) = 7817$ J

$$\text{Ba(OH)}_2(aq) + 2\text{HNO}_3(aq) \rightarrow \text{Ba(NO}_3)_2(aq) + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$$

$n(\text{Ba(OH)}_2) = 0.564 \times 0.1500 = 0.0846$ mol (limiting), $n(\text{HNO}_3) = 1.25 \times 0.400 = 0.500$ mol (excess).

$n(\text{H}_2\text{O}) = 2 \times 0.0846 = 0.1692$ mol

$$\Delta H = -\frac{7.817\ \text{kJ}}{0.1692\ \text{mol}} = -46.2\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$

questions.question: 150.0 mL of a 0.564 mol L$^{-1}$ barium hydroxide solution was placed in a well-insulated beaker. The temperature of the solution was 20.3°C. Subsequently, 400 mL of a 1.25 mol L$^{-1}$ nitric acid solution was placed in another beaker and brought to the same temperature. The two solutions were then mixed, and the final maximum temperature was recorded to be 23.7°C. Assume that the density of the solutions was 1.00 g mL$^{-1}$ (and the specific heat capacity $4.18 \times 10^{3}$ J kg$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$). A student repeated this experiment with the same volume and concentration of barium hydroxide solution, but this time used 400 mL of 1.25 mol L$^{-1}$ hydrochloric acid. The initial temperature of the solutions was once again 20.3°C. Predict if the final temperature would be higher, lower or the same as the original reaction and justify your response.
questions.answer:
The final temperature would be the same (23.7°C).

HCl, like $\text{HNO}_3$, is a strong monoprotic acid, so it is completely ionised in solution, and it is again in excess. Barium hydroxide is still the limiting reagent, so the same number of moles of water (0.1692 mol) is formed from $\text{H}^+ + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{O}$. The same amount of energy is released into the same total mass of solution, so the temperature rise is the same.

questions.question:
Sodium laurylbenzene sulfonate is used as a detergent in cleaning products and in pesticides. Its structure is shown: a chain of twelve carbons, $\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_{11}-$, attached to a benzene ring, which is attached to the anionic group $-\text{O}-\text{SO}_2-\text{O}^-\ \text{Na}^+$.

With reference to its structure, explain the cleaning action of sodium laurylbenzene sulfonate.
questions.answer:
In water, sodium laurylbenzene sulfonate dissociates into $\text{Na}^+$ ions and laurylbenzene sulfonate anions.

Each anion has two distinct parts. The long hydrocarbon chain (with the benzene ring) is non-polar (hydrophobic), so it forms dispersion forces with, and dissolves in, non-polar oil and grease. The sulfonate group, $-\text{O}-\text{SO}_2-\text{O}^-$, is anionic and polar (hydrophilic), so it forms ion–dipole attractions with water molecules and dissolves in water.

When the detergent is added to greasy dirt, the non-polar tails embed in the oil droplet while the charged heads remain in the water. With agitation, the oil is lifted off the surface and surrounded by detergent anions to form micelles. The negatively charged micelle surfaces repel each other, so the oil droplets stay suspended (emulsified) in the water and are washed away.

questions.question:
The structural formulae for compounds A, B and C are shown:

- A: $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}-\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$
- B: $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C(OH)}-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$
- C: $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}-\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$

Describe how you could distinguish between the compounds using simple reactions in a school laboratory. Include relevant reagents and observations in your response.
questions.answer:
A is a primary alcohol (2,2-dimethylpropan-1-ol), B is a tertiary alcohol (2-methylbutan-2-ol) and C is a carboxylic acid (3,3-dimethylbutanoic acid).

1. Add a small amount of sodium carbonate (or sodium hydrogen carbonate) solution to a sample of each. Only the carboxylic acid C reacts, producing bubbles (effervescence) of carbon dioxide gas:
$$2\text{RCOOH} + \text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3 \rightarrow 2\text{RCOONa} + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{CO}_2$$
The two alcohols show no bubbles.

2. To fresh samples of the two remaining compounds, add acidified potassium permanganate solution and warm gently. The primary alcohol A is oxidised (to an aldehyde/carboxylic acid), so the purple permanganate is decolourised. The tertiary alcohol B cannot be oxidised, so the solution stays purple. (Acidified potassium dichromate could be used instead: orange → green for A, stays orange for B.)

questions.question:
The structural formulae for compounds A, B and C are shown:

- A: $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}-\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$
- B: $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C(OH)}-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$
- C: $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}-\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$

Compounds A and B are isomers ($\text{C}_5\text{H}_{12}\text{O}$). Draw FIVE other isomers of this compound and provide their IUPAC names.
questions.answer:
Any five of the following alcohols (not A or B), drawn as full structural formulae:

| Condensed structural formula | IUPAC name |
|---|---|
| $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ | pentan-1-ol |
| $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH(OH)CH}_3$ | pentan-2-ol |
| $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH(OH)CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ | pentan-3-ol |
| $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCH(OH)CH}_3$ | 3-methylbutan-2-ol |
| $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ | 3-methylbutan-1-ol |
| $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH(CH}_3)\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ | 2-methylbutan-1-ol |

The diagram shows five of them drawn in full.

questions.question:
Gases $\text{A}_2$ and $\text{B}_2$ react according to the equation:

$$\text{A}_2(g) + 2\text{B}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{AB}_2(g) \qquad \Delta H < 0$$

A mixture of $\text{A}_2$ and $\text{B}_2$ was placed into a sealed vessel. The initial concentration of $\text{A}_2$ was 1.4 mol L$^{-1}$ and the initial concentration of $\text{B}_2$ was 1.0 mol L$^{-1}$. At 5 minutes, the system had reached equilibrium where the concentration of $\text{A}_2$ was 1.2 mol L$^{-1}$. The system remained at equilibrium until at 10 minutes the temperature of the system was reduced. At 15 minutes, the system re-established equilibrium.

On a graph of concentration (0–1.6 mol L$^{-1}$) against time (0–20 min), draw a trendline for each of the chemical species involved in this equilibrium to show their changes in concentration over time. Include a key.
questions.answer:
- **0–5 min:** $[\text{A}_2]$ falls from 1.4 to 1.2 mol L$^{-1}$ (a change of 0.2), so by the 1 : 2 : 2 mole ratio $[\text{B}_2]$ falls by 0.4 from 1.0 to 0.6 mol L$^{-1}$ and $[\text{AB}_2]$ rises by 0.4 from 0 to 0.4 mol L$^{-1}$. The curves are steepest at the start and flatten off (rate slows) as equilibrium is reached at 5 min.
- **5–10 min:** all three lines are horizontal (equilibrium).
- **10–15 min:** the forward reaction is exothermic, so lowering the temperature shifts the equilibrium to the right. There is no sudden jump; $[\text{A}_2]$ and $[\text{B}_2]$ decrease gradually and $[\text{AB}_2]$ increases gradually, in the ratio 1 : 2 : 2 (e.g. $\text{A}_2$ 1.2 → 1.1, $\text{B}_2$ 0.6 → 0.4, $\text{AB}_2$ 0.4 → 0.6 mol L$^{-1}$).
- **15–20 min:** all lines horizontal again (new equilibrium).

questions.question:
Gases $\text{A}_2$ and $\text{B}_2$ react according to the equation:

$$\text{A}_2(g) + 2\text{B}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{AB}_2(g) \qquad \Delta H < 0$$

A mixture of $\text{A}_2$ and $\text{B}_2$ was placed into a sealed vessel. The initial concentration of $\text{A}_2$ was 1.4 mol L$^{-1}$ and the initial concentration of $\text{B}_2$ was 1.0 mol L$^{-1}$. At 5 minutes, the system had reached equilibrium where the concentration of $\text{A}_2$ was 1.2 mol L$^{-1}$. The system remained at equilibrium until at 10 minutes the temperature of the system was reduced. At 15 minutes, the system re-established equilibrium.

Calculate $K_{eq}$ at 7 minutes.
questions.answer:
At 7 minutes the system is at the first equilibrium: $[\text{A}_2] = 1.2$, $[\text{B}_2] = 1.0 - 2(0.2) = 0.6$ and $[\text{AB}_2] = 2(0.2) = 0.4$ mol L$^{-1}$.

$$K_{eq} = \frac{[\text{AB}_2]^2}{[\text{A}_2][\text{B}_2]^2} = \frac{0.4^2}{1.2 \times 0.6^2} = 0.37$$

questions.question: 0.050 mol of ethanoic acid was reacted with 0.050 mol of ethanol in 100 mL of solution at a certain temperature. The reaction mixture was then cooled, and the excess ethanoic acid was titrated, needing 34 mL of 0.50 mol L$^{-1}$ NaOH for neutralisation. Draw the structural formulae of the products formed in the reaction between ethanoic acid and ethanol.
questions.answer:
The products are ethyl ethanoate, $\text{CH}_3\text{COOCH}_2\text{CH}_3$ (the ester), and water, $\text{H}_2\text{O}$:

$$\text{CH}_3\text{COOH} + \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH} \rightleftharpoons \text{CH}_3\text{COOCH}_2\text{CH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

questions.question: 0.050 mol of ethanoic acid was reacted with 0.050 mol of ethanol in 100 mL of solution at a certain temperature. The reaction mixture was then cooled, and the excess ethanoic acid was titrated, needing 34 mL of 0.50 mol L$^{-1}$ NaOH for neutralisation. What reagent could be added to act as a catalyst for this reaction?
questions.answer: A few drops of concentrated sulfuric acid.

questions.question: 0.050 mol of ethanoic acid was reacted with 0.050 mol of ethanol in 100 mL of solution at a certain temperature. The reaction mixture was then cooled, and the excess ethanoic acid was titrated, needing 34 mL of 0.50 mol L$^{-1}$ NaOH for neutralisation. Identify a laboratory technique that could be used to help this reaction reach equilibrium quicker and provide another advantage of using this technique.
questions.answer: Refluxing — heating the mixture with a vertical condenser fitted to the flask — allows the mixture to be heated (increasing the reaction rate) for a long time. Another advantage is that volatile (and flammable) reactants and products condense and return to the flask instead of escaping, so no material is lost and the risk of fire from vapours is reduced.

questions.question: 0.050 mol of ethanoic acid was reacted with 0.050 mol of ethanol in 100 mL of solution at a certain temperature. The reaction mixture was then cooled, and the excess ethanoic acid was titrated, needing 34 mL of 0.50 mol L$^{-1}$ NaOH for neutralisation. Calculate the equilibrium constant for this reaction.
questions.answer:
$n(\text{NaOH}) = 0.034 \times 0.50 = 0.017$ mol, so $n(\text{CH}_3\text{COOH})_{eq} = 0.017$ mol (1 : 1 reaction).

$[\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}]_{eq} = 0.017/0.100 = 0.17$ mol L$^{-1}$; initially $[\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}] = [\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}] = 0.050/0.100 = 0.50$ mol L$^{-1}$.

| | $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ | $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}$ | $\text{CH}_3\text{COOC}_2\text{H}_5$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| Initial | 0.50 | 0.50 | 0 |
| Change | $-0.33$ | $-0.33$ | $+0.33$ |
| Equilibrium | 0.17 | 0.17 | 0.33 |

Treating water as the solvent (so it is left out of the expression):

$$K_{eq} = \frac{[\text{CH}_3\text{COOC}_2\text{H}_5]}{[\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}][\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}]} = \frac{0.33}{0.17^2} = 11$$

*(If water is instead treated as a product, $[\text{H}_2\text{O}] = 0.33$ mol L$^{-1}$ is included and $K_{eq} = \dfrac{0.33^2}{0.17^2} = 3.8$; the school's marking guidelines used the first approach.)*

questions.question:
The structural diagram shows a section of polymer A:

$$-\text{CO}-\text{O}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{O}-\text{CO}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CO}-\text{O}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{O}-\text{CO}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CO}-\text{O}-$$

Draw the monomers for polymer A.
questions.answer: Polymer A is a polyester formed by condensation polymerisation. Its monomers are the diol propane-1,3-diol, $\text{HO}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{OH}$, and the dicarboxylic acid propanedioic acid, $\text{HOOC}-\text{CH}_2-\text{COOH}$.

questions.question:
The structural diagram shows a section of polymer A:

$$-\text{CO}-\text{O}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{O}-\text{CO}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CO}-\text{O}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{O}-\text{CO}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CO}-\text{O}-$$

The monomers of polymer A are propane-1,3-diol ($\text{C}_3\text{H}_8\text{O}_2$) and propanedioic acid ($\text{C}_3\text{H}_4\text{O}_4$). Determine the molar mass of a section of polymer A that consists of 40 monomers.
questions.answer:
$M(\text{C}_3\text{H}_8\text{O}_2) = 3(12.01) + 8(1.008) + 2(16.00) = 76.094$ g mol$^{-1}$

$M(\text{C}_3\text{H}_4\text{O}_4) = 3(12.01) + 4(1.008) + 4(16.00) = 104.062$ g mol$^{-1}$

40 monomers = 20 of each, alternating. Joining 40 monomers in a chain forms 39 ester links, each eliminating one water molecule ($M = 18.016$):

$$M = 20(76.094 + 104.062) - 39(18.016) = 3603.12 - 702.62 = 2900\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$$

(Equivalently: 20 repeating units of 144.124 g mol$^{-1}$ plus H and OH on the chain ends: $20(144.124) + 18.016 = 2900$ g mol$^{-1}$.)

questions.question:
A reaction flow chart is described below. Complete it by answering each part.

- But-2-ene reacts with reagent X to form $\text{C}_4\text{H}_9\text{Br}$.
- $\text{C}_4\text{H}_9\text{Br}$ reacts with $\text{OH}^-$ to form compound D.
- Compound D reacts with reagent Y to form butan-2-one.
- Propanal reacts with reagent Z to form $\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\text{O}_2$.
- $\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\text{O}_2$ reacts with $\text{NH}_3$ to form compound E.
- $\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\text{O}_2$ reacts with compound D to form compound F.

Identify reagents X, Y and Z; draw the structural formula and give the IUPAC name of $\text{C}_4\text{H}_9\text{Br}$, D, $\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\text{O}_2$ and E; and draw the structural formula of F.
questions.answer:
- **Reagent X:** hydrogen bromide, HBr.
- **$\text{C}_4\text{H}_9\text{Br}$:** $\text{CH}_3\text{CHBrCH}_2\text{CH}_3$, 2-bromobutane.
- **D:** substitution of Br by OH gives $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, butan-2-ol.
- **Reagent Y:** acidified potassium permanganate ($\text{H}^+/\text{MnO}_4^-$) or acidified potassium dichromate ($\text{H}^+/\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}$) — oxidises the secondary alcohol to the ketone.
- **Reagent Z:** acidified $\text{MnO}_4^-$ or acidified $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}$ (oxidises the aldehyde).
- **$\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\text{O}_2$:** $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$, propanoic acid.
- **E:** $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CONH}_2$, propanamide.
- **F:** the ester formed from propanoic acid and butan-2-ol, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COO}-\text{CH(CH}_3)\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ (butan-2-yl propanoate).

*(The original paper printed the bromoalkane as $\text{C}_4\text{H}_7\text{Br}$; addition of HBr to but-2-ene gives $\text{C}_4\text{H}_9\text{Br}$, as in the marking guidelines' answer 2-bromobutane, so the formula has been corrected.)*

questions.question: During a titration, which piece of glassware should be used to transfer a 25 mL aliquot of a substance to the conical flask?
questions.answer: An aliquot (an accurately known fixed volume) is delivered with a **volumetric pipette** (A). (B) is a burette, (C) a measuring cylinder and (D) a volumetric flask.

questions.question: What is the systematic name for the molecule shown?
questions.answer: The nitrogen carries an ethyl group, a propyl group and a hydrogen, so it is a secondary amine. The longest chain attached to N (propyl) is the parent amine and the ethyl group is the $N$-substituent: $N$-ethylpropanamine ($N$-ethylpropan-1-amine). There is no C=O, so it is not an amide.

questions.question:
Consider the following equilibrium system:

$$\text{N}_2(g) + 3\text{H}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NH}_3(g) \qquad \Delta H = -92\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$

Which set of conditions will produce the highest yield of ammonia?
questions.answer: The forward reaction is exothermic, so a low temperature shifts the equilibrium to the right; it also reduces the number of moles of gas (4 → 2), so high pressure shifts it to the right (Le Chatelier's principle).

questions.question: Which of the following is a **position** isomer of pentan-2-one?
questions.answer: A position isomer has the same carbon chain and functional group, with the functional group in a different position. (A) is pentan-3-one. (B) 3-methylbutan-2-one is a chain isomer; (C) cyclopentanol and (D) an enol are not ketones with the same chain.

questions.question: Which analytical technique relies on particles being initially ionised?
questions.answer: In mass spectrometry the sample molecules are first ionised (e.g. by electron bombardment) so that the ions can be accelerated and deflected according to their mass-to-charge ratio.

questions.question:
Consider the following equilibrium reaction in an aqueous solution:

$$\text{Fe}^{3+}(aq) + \text{SCN}^-(aq) \rightleftharpoons [\text{Fe(SCN)}]^{2+}(aq)$$

At 298 K, the equilibrium constant, $K_{eq}$, for the reaction is 200. A student prepares a solution containing 0.12 mol L$^{-1}$ Fe$^{3+}(aq)$ ions and 0.12 mol L$^{-1}$ SCN$^-(aq)$ ions at equilibrium.

What is the equilibrium concentration of $[\text{Fe(SCN)}]^{2+}(aq)$ at 298 K?
questions.answer: $K_{eq} = \dfrac{[\text{Fe(SCN)}^{2+}]}{[\text{Fe}^{3+}][\text{SCN}^-]}$, so $[\text{Fe(SCN)}^{2+}] = 200 \times 0.12 \times 0.12 = 2.88 \approx 2.9$ mol L$^{-1}$.

questions.question:
HInd is an acid–base indicator used in titration that exists in two equilibrium forms when dissolved in water.

$$\underset{\text{yellow}}{\text{HInd}(aq)} + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightleftharpoons \text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq) + \underset{\text{purple}}{\text{Ind}^-(aq)}$$

Which statement(s) are correct?

i. In a strongly acidic solution, yellow is observed.

ii. When the concentration of HInd$(aq)$ is less than the concentration of Ind$^-(aq)$, yellow is observed.

iii. The concentrations of HInd$(aq)$ and Ind$^-(aq)$ are approximately equal at the end point of a titration.
questions.answer: (i) High $[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]$ shifts the equilibrium left, so yellow HInd dominates — true. (ii) If $[\text{Ind}^-] > [\text{HInd}]$ the solution appears purple — false. (iii) The end point is where the indicator changes colour, i.e. where $[\text{HInd}] \approx [\text{Ind}^-]$ — true.

questions.question: Which organic molecule could have produced this infrared spectrum?
questions.answer: There is a strong, broad absorption centred near 3350 cm$^{-1}$ (alcohol O–H) and no C=O absorption at 1680–1750 cm$^{-1}$, which rules out butan-2-one and butanoic acid (whose acid O–H band would also be much broader, 2500–3000 cm$^{-1}$). But-2-ene has no O–H. So the molecule is butan-2-ol.

questions.question:
Consider the following equilibrium system:

$$2\text{ICl}(s) \rightleftharpoons \text{I}_2(s) + \text{Cl}_2(g) \qquad \Delta H = +17\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$

Which of the following changes will increase the chemical amount, in moles, of chlorine that can be produced?
options: Removing some of the solid I$_2$.
Removing the Cl$_2$ gas as it is formed.
questions.answer: $K_{eq} = [\text{Cl}_2]$ — the solids do not appear in the expression, so adding or removing solids does not shift the equilibrium. Removing Cl$_2$ lowers $[\text{Cl}_2]$ below $K_{eq}$, so the system shifts right to produce more Cl$_2$. Decreasing the temperature favours the exothermic (reverse) reaction.

questions.question: Photosynthesis is a highly endothermic reaction. Which of the following is true for the equilibrium constant, $K_{eq}$, at low temperatures?
questions.answer: For a highly endothermic reaction, low temperatures favour the reactants (the reverse, exothermic direction), so very little product is present at equilibrium and $K_{eq} \ll 1$ (but never exactly 0).

questions.question: Which peak would you find in a mass spectrum for propanal but not in a mass spectrum for propan-2-one?
questions.answer: Both have $M = 58$ and can give CH$_3^+$ (15). Propan-2-one, CH$_3$COCH$_3$, fragments to CH$_3$CO$^+$ (43). Propanal, CH$_3$CH$_2$CHO, can lose CHO or C$_2$H$_5$ to give CH$_3$CH$_2^+$ / CHO$^+$ at $m/z = 29$; propan-2-one has no C$_2$H$_5$ or CHO group, so it cannot give 29.

questions.question:
Ibuprofen is a drug used for pain relief. Chemical tests were performed on a sample of ibuprofen and the results of the tests are given below.

| Chemical test | Result with ibuprofen |
|---|---|
| Aqueous sodium carbonate | Effervescence |
| Bromine water | Solution remained orange |
| Acidified potassium permanganate | Solution remained purple |

Which functional group must be present in a molecule of ibuprofen?
questions.answer: Effervescence (CO$_2$) with sodium carbonate shows a carboxylic acid. Bromine water not decolourising rules out C=C, and permanganate not decolourising rules out a primary/secondary alcohol O–H (and C=C).

questions.question: A 0.15 mol L$^{-1}$ sample of hydrofluoric acid, HF, has a pH of 2.00. Calculate the $K_a$ of hydrofluoric acid.
In a glucose fermentation reaction, 1.50 g of ethanol was produced. What volume of carbon dioxide (measured at 25 °C and 100 kPa) was also produced in this reaction?
questions.answer: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6 \rightarrow 2\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH} + 2\text{CO}_2$, so $n(\text{CO}_2) = n(\text{ethanol}) = \dfrac{1.50}{46.068} = 0.03256$ mol. $V = 0.03256 \times 24.79 = 0.807$ L.

questions.question:
Which combination of organic reactant and reaction conditions could be used to produce 2-bromohexane as the sole product in a single step?

| | Organic reactant | Reaction conditions |
|---|---|---|
| (A) | hex-2-ene | Br$_2(l)$, room temperature |
| (B) | hex-2-ene | dilute H$_2$SO$_4(aq)$, heat |
| (C) | hex-3-ene | HBr$(g)$, room temperature |
| (D) | 2-bromohex-3-ene | H$_2(g)$, Pd/C catalyst, heat |
questions.answer: Hydrogenating the C=C of 2-bromohex-3-ene gives only 2-bromohexane. (A) gives 2,3-dibromohexane, (B) gives hexanols, and (C) gives 3-bromohexane.

questions.question: Which statement is true for both ethanol and ethanal? They both produce:
options: A molecular ion peak at $m/z = 46$ in mass spectrometry.
A sharp peak between 1680–1750 cm$^{-1}$ in IR spectroscopy.
questions.answer: Each molecule has two carbon environments, so two $^{13}$C NMR peaks. Ethanal has $M = 44$ (not 46), ethanol has no C=O, and ethanol has three $^1$H environments (CH$_3$, CH$_2$, OH).

questions.question:
Aqueous dilution of IO$_4^-$ results in the following reaction:

$$\text{IO}_4^-(aq) + 4\text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightleftharpoons \text{H}_4\text{IO}_6^-(aq) \qquad K_{eq} = 3.5 \times 10^{-2}$$

50.0 mL of a 0.896 mol L$^{-1}$ solution of KIO$_4(aq)$ is diluted to 250.0 mL with water. How many moles of H$_4$IO$_6^-(aq)$ are present at equilibrium?
questions.answer: Initial $[\text{IO}_4^-] = \dfrac{0.896 \times 0.0500}{0.2500} = 0.1792$ mol L$^{-1}$. Water is omitted from $K_{eq}$: $\dfrac{x}{0.1792 - x} = 0.035 \Rightarrow x = \dfrac{0.035 \times 0.1792}{1.035} = 6.06 \times 10^{-3}$ mol L$^{-1}$. Moles $= 6.06 \times 10^{-3} \times 0.2500 = 1.51 \times 10^{-3}$ mol. (Option B is the concentration, not the amount.)

questions.question:
A section of the polyester poly(3-hydroxyvalerate) is shown.

A single chain of this polymer is found to have a molar mass of 9530 g mol$^{-1}$ (calculated to 3 significant figures). How many monomer units of 3-hydroxyvaleric acid were required to make a chain with this molar mass?
questions.answer: Monomer 3-hydroxypentanoic acid, C$_5$H$_{10}$O$_3$ ($M = 118.13$). Each condensation releases one water, so the repeating unit is C$_5$H$_8$O$_2$ ($M = 100.12$) and a chain of $n$ units has $M = 100.12n + 18.02$ (one H and one OH at the chain ends). $100.12n + 18.02 = 9530 \Rightarrow n = 95.0$.

questions.question:
Calculate the mass of solid ammonium chloride that must be added to 25.0 mL of water to make a solution with a pH of 4.85.

p$K_a$ of NH$_4^+$ is 9.24. $MM$ of NH$_4$Cl is 53.492 g mol$^{-1}$.

A data logger was used to measure the pH changes during a titration. Hydrochloric acid with a concentration of 0.1024 mol L$^{-1}$ was added to a solution of sodium carbonate that was contaminated with sodium chloride. The titration curve is shown.

The mass and density of the mixture of sodium carbonate and sodium chloride solution aliquot used was 36.98 g and 2.360 g mL$^{-1}$ respectively. What was the concentration of sodium carbonate in the solution?
questions.answer: The first equivalence point ($\text{CO}_3^{2-} + \text{H}^+ \rightarrow \text{HCO}_3^-$) is at 29 mL (the second, at 58 mL, is twice this). $n(\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3) = n(\text{HCl to 1st equivalence}) = 0.1024 \times 0.0290 = 2.970 \times 10^{-3}$ mol. Aliquot volume $= \dfrac{36.98}{2.360} = 15.67$ mL. $c = \dfrac{2.970 \times 10^{-3}}{0.01567} = 0.1895$ mol L$^{-1}$.

questions.question:
Consider the following reaction at 300 K.

$$2\text{NO}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NO}(g) + \text{O}_2(g)$$

Write the $K_{eq}$ expression for the reaction.
questions.answer: $$K_{eq} = \frac{[\text{NO}]^2[\text{O}_2]}{[\text{NO}_2]^2}$$

questions.question:
Consider the following reaction at 300 K.

$$2\text{NO}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NO}(g) + \text{O}_2(g)$$

1.00 mol of NO$_2(g)$ is placed into a 2.00 L container and the system was allowed to reach equilibrium. At equilibrium, the concentration of NO$_2(g)$ was found to be 0.250 mol L$^{-1}$.

Calculate the equilibrium concentrations of NO$(g)$ and O$_2(g)$ at 300 K.

Consider the following reaction at 300 K.

$$2\text{NO}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NO}(g) + \text{O}_2(g)$$

1.00 mol of NO$_2(g)$ is placed into a 2.00 L container and the system was allowed to reach equilibrium. At equilibrium, the concentration of NO$_2(g)$ was found to be 0.250 mol L$^{-1}$.

Using the equilibrium concentrations $[\text{NO}] = 0.250$ mol L$^{-1}$ and $[\text{O}_2] = 0.125$ mol L$^{-1}$, calculate the equilibrium constant, $K_{eq}$, at this temperature.
questions.answer:
$$K_{eq} = \frac{[\text{NO}]^2[\text{O}_2]}{[\text{NO}_2]^2} = \frac{(0.250)^2(0.125)}{(0.250)^2} = 0.125$$

(3 significant figures, matching the data.)

questions.question:
Propene readily undergoes hydration (H$^+$/H$_2$O) to produce a mixture of two products, **A** and **B**. Compound **B** is propan-2-ol, CH$_3$CH(OH)CH$_3$. When separated, **A** and **B** are each oxidised with acidified dichromate (H$^+$/Cr$_2$O$_7^{2-}$, heat under reflux) to produce **C** and **D** respectively, where **D** is propanone (shown in the reaction scheme).

Draw the structures of **A** and **C**, and state the names of **A**, **B**, **C** and **D**.
questions.answer:
**A**: CH$_3$CH$_2$CH$_2$OH (the OH on the end carbon) — **propan-1-ol**

**B**: CH$_3$CH(OH)CH$_3$ — **propan-2-ol**

**C**: CH$_3$CH$_2$COOH (a carboxyl group, C(=O)–OH, on the end carbon) — **propanoic acid** (a primary alcohol is oxidised to the carboxylic acid under reflux)

**D**: CH$_3$COCH$_3$ — **propanone** (a secondary alcohol is oxidised to a ketone)

questions.question: Propan-2-ol (CH$_3$CH(OH)CH$_3$) has a boiling point of 82 °C and propanone (CH$_3$COCH$_3$) has a boiling point of 56 °C. Explain why propan-2-ol has a higher boiling point than propanone.
questions.answer:
Propan-2-ol contains a hydroxyl (–OH) group, so its strongest intermolecular force is **hydrogen bonding** between the H of one molecule's O–H and a lone pair on the O of a neighbouring molecule. Propanone has a carbonyl (C=O) group but no H bonded to O, so it cannot hydrogen bond with itself; its strongest intermolecular forces are **dipole–dipole forces** between the polar C=O groups (plus dispersion forces, which are similar for the two molecules of similar size).

Hydrogen bonds are stronger than dipole–dipole forces, so **more energy is required to separate** propan-2-ol molecules into the gas phase. Therefore propan-2-ol has the higher boiling point.

questions.question:
Two pieces of cotton wool soaked in concentrated hydrochloric acid and concentrated ammonia were placed at opposite ends of a glass tube. After some time, the solutions vaporise, and the two gases react to produce a ring of white powder.

Write an equation for the reaction that occurs inside the glass tube.
questions.answer: $$\text{HCl}(g) + \text{NH}_3(g) \rightarrow \text{NH}_4\text{Cl}(s)$$

questions.question:
Two pieces of cotton wool soaked in concentrated hydrochloric acid and concentrated ammonia were placed at opposite ends of a glass tube. After some time, the solutions vaporise, and the two gases react to produce a ring of white powder.

The reaction is $\text{HCl}(g) + \text{NH}_3(g) \rightarrow \text{NH}_4\text{Cl}(s)$. State which acid–base theory explains the behaviour in this reaction and justify your answer.
questions.answer: The **Brønsted–Lowry theory**. The reaction occurs in the gas phase with no water present, so the Arrhenius theory (which needs H$^+$/OH$^-$ ions in aqueous solution) cannot describe it. In Brønsted–Lowry terms, HCl acts as an acid because it **donates a proton** (H$^+$) and NH$_3$ acts as a base because it **accepts the proton**, forming NH$_4^+$ (and Cl$^-$), which make up the ionic solid NH$_4$Cl.

questions.question:
Consider the following equilibrium reaction:

$$\text{CH}_4(g) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{CO}(g) + 3\text{H}_2(g)$$

Use collision theory to explain how a decrease in volume would affect the rates of the forward and reverse reactions initially and until equilibrium is re-established.
questions.answer:
Decreasing the volume increases the concentration (partial pressure) of every gas in the mixture. Particles collide more frequently, so the frequency of successful collisions increases for both reactants and products: **both the forward and reverse rates increase immediately**.

The reverse reaction involves 4 mol of gas particles (CO + 3H$_2$) colliding, compared with 2 mol (CH$_4$ + H$_2$O) for the forward reaction, so the increase in concentration increases the frequency of successful collisions for the reverse reaction relatively more. Initially, therefore, **the reverse rate increases more than the forward rate** (reverse rate > forward rate), and the system shifts to the left.

As the reverse reaction proceeds, [CO] and [H$_2$] decrease, so **the reverse rate gradually decreases**, while [CH$_4$] and [H$_2$O] increase, so **the forward rate gradually increases**.

When the two rates become equal again, equilibrium is re-established. **At the new equilibrium the forward and reverse rates are equal, and both are faster than at the original equilibrium** because all concentrations are higher in the smaller volume.

questions.question:
Consider the following equilibrium reaction:

$$\text{CH}_4(g) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{CO}(g) + 3\text{H}_2(g)$$

Describe how the addition of a catalyst would affect the rates of the forward and reverse reactions and the position of the equilibrium.
questions.answer: A catalyst provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy for both the forward and reverse reactions, so a greater proportion of collisions are successful in both directions. **The forward and reverse rates increase by the same factor** (equally), so equilibrium is reached faster, but **the position of equilibrium (and $K_{eq}$) is unchanged** — the equilibrium concentrations stay the same.

questions.question:
Alcohols can undergo elimination and substitution reactions under different conditions. A sample of 2-methylbutan-2-ol was subjected to an experimental set of conditions to determine whether elimination (giving 2-methylbut-2-ene) or substitution (giving 2-chloro-2-methylbutane) would occur.

The sole product of the reaction was purified and analysed using $^{13}$C NMR spectroscopy. The $^{13}$C NMR spectrum is shown below.

Deduce which of the two possible products was formed in the reaction. Explain your choice using $^{13}$C NMR data.
questions.answer:
The product is **2-methylbut-2-ene** (the elimination product).

The spectrum has two peaks well above 100 ppm (at about 118 and 132 ppm). According to the $^{13}$C NMR data sheet, shifts of about 90–150 ppm correspond to carbons in a C=C double bond, so the product contains an alkene. 2-Chloro-2-methylbutane has no C=C; its most deshielded carbon (the C–Cl carbon) would appear at about 70 ppm, so it would give no signal above 100 ppm.

*Note: the original solutions quote the alkene peaks as about 138 and 163 ppm; the spectrum shows them at about 118 and 132 ppm, within the C=C range.*

questions.question:
The graph shows the trend in standard enthalpy of combustion values (reported as $-\Delta_c H^\ominus$) for the first five alkanes (methane to pentane), in kJ mol$^{-1}$.

Explain the trend observed.
questions.answer:
As the number of carbon atoms in the alkane increases, the enthalpy of combustion ($-\Delta_c H^\ominus$) increases in a regular (approximately linear) way, by about 650 kJ mol$^{-1}$ per carbon — i.e. more heat is released per mole of alkane burned.

Each successive alkane differs by a –CH$_2$– unit. Combustion of each extra CH$_2$ unit requires breaking more C–C and C–H bonds (and O=O bonds), which is endothermic, but it also forms one extra CO$_2$ and one extra H$_2$O, and forming the strong C=O and O–H bonds in these products is exothermic.

Because the energy released in forming the bonds in the extra products is greater than the energy absorbed in breaking the extra bonds in the reactants, each additional CH$_2$ unit adds a roughly constant net amount of energy released, so more energy is released per mole of alkane combusted as the chain gets longer.

questions.question:
The graph shows the trend in standard enthalpy of combustion values (reported as $-\Delta_c H^\ominus$) for the first five alkanes (methane to pentane), in kJ mol$^{-1}$.

Using the graph, calculate the energy released from the combustion of pentane, in kJ g$^{-1}$.
questions.answer:
From the graph, for pentane (5 carbons) $-\Delta_c H^\ominus = 3500$ kJ mol$^{-1}$.

$M(\text{C}_5\text{H}_{12}) = 5(12.01) + 12(1.008) = 72.146$ g mol$^{-1}$

Energy released per gram $= \dfrac{3500}{72.146} = 48.5$ kJ g$^{-1}$

questions.question:
A beaker contains 105 mL of saturated calcium sulfate solution at 25 °C. The $K_{sp}$ for CaSO$_4$ is $4.93 \times 10^{-5}$ at 25 °C.

Calculate the molar solubility of calcium sulfate in water at this temperature.
questions.answer:
$\text{CaSO}_4(s) \rightleftharpoons \text{Ca}^{2+}(aq) + \text{SO}_4^{2-}(aq)$

Let $s$ = molar solubility, so $[\text{Ca}^{2+}] = [\text{SO}_4^{2-}] = s$.

$K_{sp} = s^2 = 4.93 \times 10^{-5} \Rightarrow s = \sqrt{4.93 \times 10^{-5}} = 7.02 \times 10^{-3}$ mol L$^{-1}$

questions.question:
A beaker contains 105 mL of saturated calcium sulfate solution at 25 °C. The $K_{sp}$ for CaSO$_4$ is $4.93 \times 10^{-5}$ at 25 °C, so its molar solubility is $7.02 \times 10^{-3}$ mol L$^{-1}$.

145 mL of 0.500 mol L$^{-1}$ sodium sulfate solution is added to the saturated calcium sulfate. Determine whether a precipitate will form and justify your answer with calculations.

The following reactions are performed at 823 K.

Reaction 1: $\text{CoO}(s) + \text{H}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{Co}(s) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(g) \qquad K_{eq1} = 67$

Reaction 2: $\text{CoO}(s) + \text{CO}(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{Co}(s) + \text{CO}_2(g) \qquad K_{eq2} = 490$

Use the information provided to calculate the value for the equilibrium constant, $K_{eq3}$, at 823 K for Reaction 3. Show your working.

Reaction 3: $\text{H}_2(g) + \text{CO}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{CO}(g) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(g) \qquad K_{eq3} = ?$
questions.answer:
Reverse reaction 2 (which inverts its constant):

$\text{Co}(s) + \text{CO}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{CoO}(s) + \text{CO}(g) \qquad K = \dfrac{1}{490}$

Add it to reaction 1 (adding equations multiplies the constants); CoO and Co cancel:

$\text{H}_2(g) + \text{CO}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{CO}(g) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(g)$

$$K_{eq3} = K_{eq1} \times \frac{1}{K_{eq2}} = \frac{67}{490} = 0.137 \;(0.14)$$

Check: $K_{eq1} = \dfrac{[\text{H}_2\text{O}]}{[\text{H}_2]}$, $K_{eq2} = \dfrac{[\text{CO}_2]}{[\text{CO}]}$, so $\dfrac{K_{eq1}}{K_{eq2}} = \dfrac{[\text{CO}][\text{H}_2\text{O}]}{[\text{H}_2][\text{CO}_2]} = K_{eq3}$.

questions.question:
For the reaction

$$\text{H}_2(g) + \text{CO}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{CO}(g) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(g)$$

the equilibrium constant is $K_{eq} = 0.137$ at 823 K. At 1973 K the value of $K_{eq}$ is 4.9. Justify whether the forward reaction is endothermic or exothermic.
questions.answer:
$K_{eq} = \dfrac{[\text{CO}][\text{H}_2\text{O}]}{[\text{H}_2][\text{CO}_2]}$ increases from 0.137 to 4.9 as the temperature increases from 823 K to 1973 K, so at higher temperature the equilibrium lies further to the right (more products).

By Le Chatelier's principle, increasing the temperature shifts an equilibrium in the direction that absorbs heat (the endothermic direction) to oppose the change. Since the forward reaction is favoured at higher temperature, **the forward reaction is endothermic**.

questions.question: Outline how infrared spectroscopy could be used to distinguish between a sample of cyclohexanone and a sample of cyclohexanol.
questions.answer:
Cyclohexanol contains an alcohol O–H group, so its IR spectrum will show a strong, **broad absorption at 3230–3550 cm$^{-1}$**; cyclohexanone has no O–H, so this absorption is absent.

Cyclohexanone contains a C=O group, so its spectrum will show a strong, **sharp absorption at 1680–1750 cm$^{-1}$**; this is absent from the cyclohexanol spectrum.

questions.question: Samples of cyclohexane (C$_6$H$_{12}$) and bromocyclohexane (C$_6$H$_{11}$Br) cannot be easily distinguished from one another using infrared spectroscopy. Suggest another analytical technique that can be used to distinguish the two and refer to any differences in the spectra.
questions.answer:
**Mass spectrometry.** Cyclohexane gives a molecular ion peak at $m/z = 84$. Bromocyclohexane gives two molecular ion peaks of approximately equal height at $m/z = 162$ and $164$, because bromine exists as two isotopes, $^{79}$Br and $^{81}$Br, in about a 1 : 1 ratio.

(Alternatively, **$^{13}$C NMR**: cyclohexane has only 1 carbon environment, so 1 peak, whereas bromocyclohexane has 4 carbon environments (C1, C2/C6, C3/C5, C4), so 4 peaks, including one shifted downfield by the C–Br.)

questions.question: Calculate the volume of water that must be added to a 220.0 mL solution of sodium hydroxide with a pH of 13.030 to achieve a solution with a final pH of 12.699 at 25 °C.

The structure of a cationic detergent, cetrimonium (a long hydrocarbon chain bonded to a positively charged trimethylammonium group, $-\text{N}^+(\text{CH}_3)_3$), is shown.

With reference to its structure, explain how cetrimonium can be used to produce a stable emulsion of oil in water.
questions.answer:
Cetrimonium has two distinct regions. The long hydrocarbon chain (16 carbons) is non-polar and **hydrophobic**; the $-\text{N}^+(\text{CH}_3)_3$ head is ionic (positively charged) and **hydrophilic**.

When the detergent is shaken with oil and water, the hydrophobic tails dissolve in the oil droplets, interacting with the non-polar oil molecules through dispersion forces. The charged heads stay at the droplet surface, projecting into the water, where they form **ion–dipole forces** with polar water molecules.

In this way the oil is broken up into tiny droplets, each surrounded by detergent molecules — a **micelle** with the oil inside and a layer of positive charges on the outside.

Because every droplet's surface is positively charged, neighbouring droplets **repel each other** and cannot coalesce into a separate oil layer, while the hydrophilic heads keep the droplets dispersed in the water. The result is a stable emulsion of oil in water.

questions.question:
Hypochlorous acid, HOCl, is a sterilising agent used in swimming pools. It is produced when chlorine reacts with water according to the equation shown.

$$\text{Cl}_2(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightleftharpoons \text{HOCl}(aq) + \text{HCl}(aq)$$

HOCl ionises to form the hypochlorite ion, OCl$^-$, which is a less effective disinfectant than the undissociated acid. The graph shows the concentrations of HOCl$(aq)$ and OCl$^-(aq)$ at different pH values at 25 °C.
